title: Encontrar el Bug
description: Identifica errores intencionales en fragmentos de codigo Java. Desarrolla tu habilidad de debugging y aprende los pitfalls mas comunes del lenguaje.

topics.title: NullPointerException y null
topics.content:
NullPointerException es la excepcion mas comun en Java y una de las causas principales de aplicaciones inestables. Ocurre cuando se intenta acceder a un metodo o campo de un objeto que tiene valor null. Este bug puede ser especialmente peligroso porque no se detecta en tiempo de compilacion y solo aparece en ejecucion, a veces en escenarios dificiles de reproducir.

Entender como prevenir y manejar null es fundamental para escribir codigo robusto. Java ofrece herramientas como Optional, Objects.requireNonNull y la anotacion @Nullable para gestionar la ausencia de valores de forma segura.

Los errores mas tipicos incluyen accesos a metodos de referencias null, cadenas de llamadas donde cualquier enlace puede ser null, y el unboxing automatico de tipos envoltorios como Integer que pueden contener null.
examples: **Acceso a metodo de referencia null:** Llamar a `length()` sobre un `String` null lanza `NullPointerException`. Solucion: agregar un null check antes de usar la referencia o usar `Optional`.

**Optional como alternativa a null:** `Optional.ofNullable(valor).orElse("default")` elimina la necesidad de null checks explicitos y fuerza al desarrollador a manejar el caso donde el valor puede no existir, haciendo el codigo mas expressivo y seguro.

**Objects.requireNonNull para validacion:** `Objects.requireNonNull(nombre, "El nombre no puede ser null")` valida argumentos null temprano y lanza `NullPointerException` con un mensaje descriptivo. Ideal para validacion de parametros en constructores y metodos.

**NPE en cadena de llamadas:** En `usuario.getDireccion().getCiudad().toUpperCase()`, cualquiera de las llamadas en la cadena puede retornar null, causando NPE en la siguiente llamada. Solucion: usar Optional en cada paso o null checks intermedios.
**Null check inutil despues de uso:** Si se ejecuta `valor.length()` antes de `if (valor != null)`, la NPE ya habria ocurrido. El orden importa: validar null antes de usar la referencia.

**Unboxing de Integer null:** El unboxing automatico de `Integer` a `int` lanza `NullPointerException` si el `Integer` es null. Aunque el tipo primitivo `int` no puede ser null, la conversion automatica falla antes de asignar el valor.

topics.title: Bugs de concurrencia
topics.content:
Los bugs de concurrencia son algunos de los mas dificiles de detectar y reproducir. Ocurren cuando multiples hilos acceden y modifican recursos compartidos sin la sincronizacion adecuada. Estos bugs pueden manifestarse intermitentemente, hacer que la app parezca estable durante pruebas pero falle en produccion.

Son extremadamente dificiles de debuggear porque dependen del scheduling del hilo, que es no determinista. Un bug de concurrencia puede aparecer una vez en mil ejecuciones, lo que hace que las pruebas unitarias tradicionales no lo capturen de forma confiable.

Dominar los conceptos de concurrencia es esencial para sistemas multi-hilo. Esto incluye comprender race conditions, deadlocks, livelocks, y la diferencia entre `volatile` y atomicidad real.
examples: **Race condition en contador:** El operador `++` no es atomico: es lectura + suma + escritura. Cuando multiples hilos lo ejecutan simultaneamente, pueden leer el mismo valor, incrementarlo y escribir el mismo resultado, perdiendo actualizaciones. Solucion: usar `AtomicInteger` o `synchronized`.

**Deadlock por orden inconsistente de locks:** Cuando dos hilos adquieren los locks en orden inverso (`lockA` luego `lockB` vs `lockB` luego `lockA`), cada uno espera que el otro libere su lock, creando un interbloqueo. Solucion: siempre adquirir los locks en el mismo orden.

**ConcurrentModificationException en ArrayList:** El iterator de `ArrayList` detecta modificaciones estructurales durante la iteracion y lanza `ConcurrentModificationException`. Solucion: usar `iterator.remove()` o `CopyOnWriteArrayList`.

**Volatile no garantiza atomicidad:** `volatile` garantiza visibilidad entre hilos pero no atomicidad. La operacion `++` sigue siendo lectura-suma-escritura y puede intercalarse con otros hilos. Solucion: usar `AtomicInteger` o `synchronized`.

**Livelock en retry infinito:** Livelock ocurre cuando los hilos cambian de estado en respuesta al otro pero ninguno progresa. A diferencia del deadlock, los hilos estan activos pero no avanzan. Solucion: backoff exponencial o retry limitado.

**Sobreescritura en coleccion no sincronizada:** `HashMap` no es thread-safe. Operaciones concurrentes pueden causar data race, corrupcion de estructura interna o perdida de datos. Solucion: usar `ConcurrentHashMap` o `Collections.synchronizedMap()`.

topics.title: Memory leaks y garbage collection
topics.content:
Aunque Java tiene garbage collection automatica, las memory leaks siguen siendo un problema real. Ocurren cuando objetos ya no necesarios permanecen referenciados y no pueden ser recolectados. Los culpables mas comunes son: colecciones estaticas que crecen indefinidamente, recursos no cerrados como streams y conexiones, y listeners no removidos.

Estos problemas se manifiestan como `OutOfMemoryError` o degradacion gradual del rendimiento en aplicaciones de larga duracion. A diferencia de los leaks en C/C++, en Java el objeto no se pierde de memoria sino que simplemente no se puede liberar porque todavia tiene referencias activas.

La prevencion implica buenas practicas como usar try-with-resources, limitar el tamano de caches, remover listeners cuando ya no se necesitan, y evitar el estado estatico mutable.
examples: **Coleccion estatica que crece sin control:** Los objetos estaticos no son recolectados por el GC mientras viva la clase. Un `ArrayList` estatico que solo agrega nunca libera memoria, eventualmente causando `OutOfMemoryError`. Solucion: usar un cache con limite o limpiar periodicamente.

**Recurso no cerrado - FileInputStream:** `FileInputStream` mantiene un handle del sistema operativo. Si no se cierra, el recurso queda retenido. Solucion: usar try-with-resources para garantizar el cierre automatico.

**try-with-resources correcto:** `try (FileInputStream fis = new FileInputStream("datos.txt"))` garantiza que el recurso se cierre al finalizar el bloque, ya sea por exito o excepcion. Es la forma recomendada de manejar `AutoCloseable` en Java 7+.

**Listener registrado pero nunca removido:** Si un objeto registra listeners en un componente de larga vida y nunca los remueve, el componente retiene referencia al objeto impidiendo su garbage collection. Solucion: remover listeners en `dispose()` o usar `WeakReference`.

**WeakReference para caches:** `SoftReference` permite que el GC recolecte el objeto cuando memoria es escasa, pero lo retenga mientras haya espacio. Es ideal para caches donde el objeto es costly de crear pero no critico mantener.

**finalize() poco confiable:** `finalize()` no tiene garantia de ejecucion ni de timing. El GC puede nunca llamarlo, o hacerlo mucho despues de que el recurso ya no se necesita. Solucion: usar try-with-resources o `Cleaner` de Java 9+.

topics.title: Bugs logicos y algoritmicos
topics.content:
Los bugs logicos son errores en el diseno o implementacion de un algoritmo que producen resultados incorrectos sin lanzar excepciones. Son los mas peligrosos porque pasan desapercibidos en pruebas basicas y pueden causar corrupcion de datos, decisiones incorrectas o comportamiento inesperado.

Incluyen errores off-by-one, overflow de enteros, comparaciones de strings con `==`, y problemas con el contrato `equals`/`hashCode`. Estos bugs requieren atencion al detalle y comprension profunda del lenguaje para ser detectados.

A diferencia de los errores de compilacion o runtime, los bugs logicos no generan ningun tipo de advertencia. El programa compila y ejecuta sin problemas, pero produce resultados equivocados que pueden pasar desapercibidos por mucho tiempo.
examples: **Off-by-one en bucle:** Usar `i <= numeros.length` en lugar de `i < numeros.length` causa `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` en la ultima iteracion. El indice valido va de 0 a `length-1`. Solucion: cambiar `<=` por `<`.

**Comparacion de strings con ==:** El operador `==` compara referencias de memoria, no contenido. Dos objetos `String` creados con `new` tienen diferentes referencias aunque tengan el mismo texto. Solucion: usar `a.equals(b)` para comparar contenido.

**Integer overflow silencioso:** `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1` causa overflow y el resultado es `Integer.MIN_VALUE` sin ningun error. Esto puede causar bugs logicos graves en calculos financieros o indices. Solucion: usar `Math.addExact()` para detectar overflow.

**Contrato equals/hashCode roto:** Si `equals()` es overridden, `hashCode()` tambien debe serlo. De lo contrario, objetos iguales pueden tener diferentes hashes, causando comportamiento inesperado en `HashMap`, `HashSet` y otras colecciones que dependen del hash.

**Mutable static state compartido:** El estado estatico mutable es compartido por todos los hilos y clases. Puede causar efectos secundarios inesperados, problemas de concurrencia y hace que el codigo sea dificil de testear. Solucion: inyeccion de dependencias o configuracion inmutable.

**Problema de serializacion:** Un campo marcado como `transient` no se serializa. Al deserializar, ese campo sera null aunque el objeto original lo tenia. Si el campo debe persistir, no debe ser transient; si es sensible, debe manejarse por separado.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about String comparison with ==
options: The first string is created with the literal syntax
The second string is created with the literal syntax
Comparing strings with == checks content equality, but for new String() objects it compares references, so this always returns false
questions.explanation: The operator == compares object references, not content. 'new String("hello")' creates a new object on the heap, while string literals are interned. Two distinct String objects created with new will have different references even if their content is identical. Fix: use s1.equals(s2) to compare content.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about off-by-one in array loop
options: The array initialization is correct
The loop starts at index 0, which is correct
Using i <= arr.length causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on the last iteration
questions.explanation: Array indices in Java are 0-based, so valid indices are 0 to arr.length - 1. Using <= instead of < causes the loop to access arr[arr.length], which is out of bounds. Fix: change the condition to i < arr.length.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about NullPointerException on unboxing
options: The Integer object is initialized correctly
The method call to intValue() returns the primitive
Unboxing a null Integer to int causes NullPointerException, not the division
questions.explanation: When a null Integer is unboxed to int (or used in arithmetic), Java attempts to call intValue() on null, causing NullPointerException. The null check after arithmetic is too late. Fix: check for null before the operation, or use Integer objects directly with null-safe methods.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about switch statement missing break
options: The switch expression evaluates the grade correctly
The default case handles unexpected values
Missing break causes fall-through: grade 'B' also executes the 'A' case
questions.explanation: Without break statements, switch cases fall through to subsequent cases. When grade is 'B', it executes the 'A' block and then the 'B' block because there is no break after case 'A'. Fix: add break after each case body.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about StringBuilder reuse
options: The StringBuilder is created correctly
The append method adds text correctly
Using System.out.println(sb) prints the StringBuilder's internal buffer, but sb is not reset, so subsequent appends accumulate
questions.explanation: StringBuilder sb is created once and reused. After printing, the internal buffer still contains 'Hello '. The next append adds 'World' to the same buffer, so it prints 'Hello World' instead of just 'World'. Fix: create a new StringBuilder inside the loop or call sb.setLength(0) to reset it.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about variable scope with nested blocks
options: The outer variable count is initialized correctly
The inner loop modifies count as expected
Declaring int i inside the for-loop means it is scoped to that block; this code compiles and runs correctly
questions.explanation: This question highlights a common misconception. Both for-loops declare their own i variable, which is block-scoped. There is no bug here — the code compiles and runs. However, if someone tries to access i from the outer loop inside the inner loop (or vice versa), it would fail. The correct answer is that the code works as written.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about exception handling with try-catch-finally
options: The try block reads the file correctly
The catch block handles the exception
The finally block throws an IOException which masks the original FileNotFoundException
questions.explanation: If br.close() in the finally block throws an IOException (e.g., because br is null or already closed with an error), it overwrites the original FileNotFoundException from the try block. This loses the root cause. Fix: use try-with-resources to ensure automatic resource closing, or add a try-catch inside finally.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about autoboxing and Integer cache
options: Both Integer objects are created from the value 127
The comparison returns true because both reference the cached Integer
Using == on boxed Integer values beyond the cache range (-128 to 127) compares references, not values
questions.explanation: Java caches Integer objects for values between -128 and 127. For a=127, both variables reference the same cached object, so a==b is true. But b=200 is outside the cache range, so a==b compares two different Integer references and returns false. Fix: use equals() for Integer comparison.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about String immutability and concatenation in a loop
options: The initial string is created correctly
The loop appends each element
Concatenating strings in a loop creates a new String object each iteration, causing O(n^2) time and excessive memory allocation
questions.explanation: Strings in Java are immutable. Each += creates a new String object and copies the content, resulting in quadratic time complexity. For large lists, this is extremely slow and memory-intensive. Fix: use StringBuilder to build the result in a loop.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about instanceof pattern matching
options: The instanceof check correctly identifies String type
The pattern variable 's' is scoped to the if block correctly
Using 's' outside the if block causes a compile error because pattern variables are scoped to the enclosing conditional
questions.explanation: Pattern variables introduced by instanceof are only in scope within the true branch of the conditional. Attempting to use 's' outside the if block is a compile-time error. Fix: declare the variable inside the if block or use explicit casting after the instanceof check.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about enum comparison
options: The enum Direction is defined correctly
The switch statement handles all enum values
Comparing enums with .equals() works but == is preferred and idiomatic for enums
questions.explanation: While d.equals(Direction.NORTH) works, == is the standard and recommended way to compare enums in Java. Enums are singletons, so == is safe and more readable. However, this is not a bug per se. The real issue is that the default case is unreachable since all enum values are handled, but this doesn't cause a bug.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about try-with-resources and suppressed exceptions
options: The try-with-resources ensures the stream is closed
The catch block handles IOException
If close() throws, the original exception from readAllBytes is suppressed and replaced
questions.explanation: When a try-with-resources block has an exception in the body AND the close() method also throws, the close() exception is added as a suppressed exception to the original. However, if the original exception is caught and a new exception is thrown in the catch block, the suppressed exception from close() is lost. Fix: catch Exception instead or handle suppressed exceptions explicitly.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about operator precedence with bitwise and logical operators
options: The variable x is initialized correctly
The condition checks if x is positive
Missing parentheses cause incorrect precedence: ! binds tighter than ==, so this checks if the negation of (x > 0) equals 1
questions.explanation: The expression !(x > 0) == 1 is evaluated as (!(x > 0)) == 1. When x=5, !(5>0) is false (0), and 0==1 is false. The intent was likely x > 0 == 1, which itself needs parentheses as (x > 0) == 1. Fix: add explicit parentheses to clarify the logic.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about String.split with regex
options: The input string is a valid CSV line
The split method returns an array of fields
The dot . in the regex is not escaped, so it matches any character instead of a literal dot
questions.explanation: In regex, the dot (.) is a wildcard that matches any character. Using split(".") will split on any character, not just literal dots. Fix: escape the dot as split("\\.") or use Pattern.quote(".").

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about using var with diamond operator
options: The var keyword infers the type correctly
The ArrayList is created with the diamond operator
Combining var with diamond operator is not allowed; var requires explicit type on the right side
questions.explanation: Java does not allow var with the diamond operator (new ArrayList<>()) because var needs the right side to infer the type. If both sides use diamond, there is no type to infer. Fix: use var list = new ArrayList<String>() or List<String> list = new ArrayList<>().

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about mutable static state in a counter
options: The static counter is shared across all instances
The increment method modifies the counter correctly
The mutable static field is not synchronized, causing race conditions in multi-threaded environments
questions.explanation: Static mutable state is shared across all threads. The increment method is not synchronized, so concurrent calls can cause lost updates (race condition). Fix: use AtomicInteger for the counter or synchronize the increment method.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about text blocks and indentation
options: The text block preserves the intended formatting
The closing triple quotes determine the indentation level
The closing triple quotes must have no leading whitespace for proper indentation
questions.explanation: In Java text blocks, the closing """ determines the indentation baseline. Any leading whitespace on the closing delimiter is used to strip indentation from the content. If the closing """ has unexpected indentation, the output may have unwanted leading spaces. Fix: ensure the closing """ is at the desired indentation level.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about switch expressions with arrow syntax
options: The switch expression uses arrow syntax correctly
The default case covers all other values
Arrow syntax does not allow fall-through, but the missing case for EVEN causes a compile error
questions.explanation: Switch expressions with arrow syntax require all cases to be covered (or a default). If the enum has EVEN and ODD, but only ODD is handled and there is no default, the compiler will complain about incomplete coverage. Fix: add a default case or handle all enum values.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about record components
options: The record Point is defined correctly
The record automatically generates constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString
Records are implicitly final and cannot be extended; attempting to subclass a record causes a compile error
questions.explanation: Records in Java are implicitly final. They cannot be subclassed. If this code tries to create a subclass of Point, it will fail to compile. Records also cannot extend other classes (they implicitly extend java.lang.Record). Fix: use composition or interfaces instead of inheritance.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about sealed classes
options: The sealed class Animal permits only Cat and Dog
Cat and Dog correctly extend Animal
The sealed class must be in the same module or package; if Dog is in a different package without 'open', it fails to compile
questions.explanation: Sealed classes restrict which classes can extend them. All permitted subclasses must be in the same module (or package, if in the unnamed module). If Dog is in a different package and the class is not open, the compiler will reject it. Fix: ensure all subclasses are in the same package/module, or use 'open' modifier.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about array copy with Arrays.copyOf
options: The original array is created correctly
The copy is created with the correct length
Arrays.copyOf creates a new array but does not copy references; inner arrays are shared, causing unintended mutations
questions.explanation: Arrays.copyOf performs a shallow copy. For a 2D array, the outer array is copied, but the inner arrays are still the same references. Modifying copy[0][0] also modifies original[0][0]. Fix: manually deep-copy each inner array or use a deep copy utility.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about instanceof with null
options: The object is initialized to null
The instanceof check correctly handles null
instanceof returns false for null, so the cast never executes, but using the pattern variable after is safe
questions.explanation: instanceof returns false when the object is null, so the pattern variable is not introduced and the cast block is not entered. This is actually correct behavior, not a bug. However, a common mistake is to assume instanceof throws an exception for null — it doesn't. The code works as expected.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about enum with abstract method
options: The enum Operation defines operations correctly
Each enum constant implements the abstract method
Enum constants are implicitly final and cannot be subclassed, so abstract enum methods work via constant-specific class bodies
questions.explanation: Enum constants with abstract methods create anonymous subclasses. Each constant (ADD, SUBTRACT) provides its own implementation. This is valid Java. The 'bug' is that if you forget to implement the abstract method for a new constant, you get a compile error. This code compiles and works correctly.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about floating point precision
options: The double values are initialized correctly
The addition performs floating point arithmetic
Floating point precision causes 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3; comparing doubles with == is unreliable
questions.explanation: IEEE 754 floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly. 0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. Comparing with == returns false. Fix: use BigDecimal for precise decimal arithmetic, or compare with a tolerance (epsilon).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about resource leak with Scanner
options: The Scanner is created to read from System.in
The hasNextLine loop reads all lines correctly
The Scanner is never closed, leaking the underlying input stream resource
questions.explanation: The Scanner wrapping System.in is never closed. While closing System.in can have side effects, not closing the Scanner can leak resources. In long-running applications, this accumulates. Fix: use try-with-resources or explicitly close the Scanner in a finally block.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about missing @Override annotation
options: The Dog class extends Animal correctly
The speak method has the correct signature
Missing @Override means a typo in the method name silently creates a new method instead of overriding
questions.explanation: Without @Override, if the method signature doesn't exactly match the parent (e.g., different parameter types or a typo), Java silently creates a new method instead of overriding. The @Override annotation causes a compile error if the override is invalid, catching mistakes early. Fix: always use @Override when overriding methods.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about calling super() in constructors
options: The superclass has a default constructor
The subclass constructor calls super() correctly
If super() is not the first statement, the code fails to compile; Java requires super() before any other code
questions.explanation: Java requires that super() or this() be the first statement in a constructor. If you put code before super(), the compiler rejects it. This ensures the parent is fully initialized before the child. Fix: move super() to be the first line, or restructure the logic.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about breaking equals/hashCode contract
options: The equals method compares email fields correctly
The hashCode method is overridden
hashCode is based on name but equals is based on email, breaking the contract
questions.explanation: The equals/hashCode contract requires that if two objects are equal (equals returns true), they must have the same hashCode. Here, equals compares email but hashCode uses name. Two Users with the same email but different names would be equal but have different hashes, causing HashMap/HashSet to malfunction. Fix: use the same fields in both methods.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about exposing internal mutable state
options: The Student class encapsulates the grades list
The constructor creates a new ArrayList correctly
Returning the mutable list directly allows external code to modify internal state
questions.explanation: getGrades() returns a direct reference to the internal grades list. External code can add/remove elements, bypassing any validation or logic in the class. Fix: return Collections.unmodifiableList(grades) or return a copy new ArrayList<>(grades).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about incorrect method signature in overriding
options: The parent class defines a protected method
The child class provides a method with the same name
The overriding method has a different parameter type (Object vs String), so it overloads instead of overriding
questions.explanation: For a method to override, the signature must match exactly (name + parameter types). The parent takes String, but the child takes Object. This creates an overloaded method, not an override. The @Override annotation would catch this. Fix: use the exact same parameter type.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about == vs equals for object comparison
options: Two Rectangle objects are created with the same dimensions
The variables r1 and r2 reference different objects
== compares references, not values, so this always returns false even with identical fields
questions.explanation: == compares object references (memory addresses), not field values. Two objects created with new are always different references. Fix: override equals() and use r1.equals(r2), or override equals with field comparison.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about abstract class instantiation
options: The abstract class Shape defines an abstract method
The Circle subclass implements draw() correctly
Instantiating an abstract class with new Shape() is not allowed; abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly
questions.explanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated with new. They serve as base classes that define a contract. Attempting new Shape() causes a compile error. Fix: instantiate a concrete subclass like new Circle(5), or use an anonymous subclass.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about interface default method conflict
options: Interface A defines a default greet() method
Interface B also defines a default greet() method
When a class implements both interfaces, the compiler requires an explicit override to resolve the conflict
questions.explanation: When a class implements two interfaces with the same default method signature, Java cannot choose one over the other. The class must provide its own implementation that explicitly calls Interface.super.method(). This is called the 'diamond problem' resolution. Fix: override greet() in the implementing class.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Liskov Substitution Principle violation
options: The Rectangle class has width, height, and setWidth methods
The Square subclass extends Rectangle
Square overrides setWidth to also change height, breaking behavioral compatibility expected by Rectangle
questions.explanation: The Liskov Substitution Principle states that subclasses must be substitutable for their parent types. If code expects a Rectangle and sets width independently of height, a Square will behave unexpectedly (changing width also changes height). This violates LSP. Fix: use composition or a separate shape hierarchy.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about static method hiding
options: The parent class has a static helper method
The child class defines a static method with the same signature
Static methods are hidden, not overridden; polymorphism does not apply to static methods
questions.explanation: Static methods are bound at compile time (static binding). When a child class defines a static method with the same signature as the parent, it hides the parent's method but does not override it. Polymorphism doesn't apply. Calling through a parent reference calls the parent's version. Fix: use instance methods for polymorphic behavior.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about circular reference in equals
options: The Node class has a reference to another Node
The equals method checks for the same instance first
The equals method calls other.equals(this) without a termination condition, causing infinite recursion
questions.explanation: When comparing node1.equals(node2), it calls node2.equals(node1), which calls node1.equals(node2), creating infinite recursion and StackOverflowError. Fix: compare fields directly instead of delegating equality back to the other object.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Builder pattern with mutable state
options: The Builder creates a User object step by step
The build method returns the constructed User
The builder stores references to mutable objects; if the caller modifies them after build, the User's state changes
questions.explanation: The Builder accepts a mutable List and stores a direct reference. If the caller modifies the list after calling build(), the User's internal state changes unexpectedly. Fix: make a defensive copy in the builder: this.roles = new ArrayList<>(roles).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about inner class and this reference
options: The outer class has a field called value
The inner class also has a field called value
this.value in the inner class refers to the inner class field, not the outer class field
questions.explanation: In an inner class, 'this' refers to the inner class instance. To access the outer class's 'value' field when there's a name collision, you must use OuterClass.this.value. Without it, the inner class field shadows the outer field. Fix: use OuterClassName.this.value.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about mutable static state in Singleton
options: The Singleton pattern uses double-checked locking
The volatile modifier prevents instruction reordering
The instance is not volatile, so another thread may see a partially constructed object
questions.explanation: Without volatile, the JVM may reorder the instance assignment and constructor execution. Thread A might see a non-null instance that hasn't finished construction yet. Fix: add volatile to the instance field declaration.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about immutable object with mutable field
options: The Person class is designed to be immutable
The fields are marked final
The mutable List field is returned by reference, allowing external modification of internal state
questions.explanation: Even though the field is final, returning the mutable list directly allows callers to modify its contents. Immutability requires defensive copying: return Collections.unmodifiableList(phones) or return new ArrayList<>(phones).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Factory method returning null
options: The factory method creates a Shape based on the type parameter
The default case returns a Circle as fallback
Returning null when type is unknown causes NullPointerException in calling code
questions.explanation: Returning null from a factory method shifts the null-handling burden to the caller. If the caller doesn't expect null, it causes NullPointerException. Fix: throw an IllegalArgumentException for unknown types, or return a default shape.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about toString not being overridden
options: The Point class stores x and y coordinates
The equals and hashCode methods are overridden
The default toString returns the class name and hash code, not the field values
questions.explanation: Without overriding toString(), printing a Point object shows something like Point@1a2b3c4 instead of Point(3,5). This makes debugging difficult. Fix: override toString() to return a meaningful representation, or use a record which generates toString automatically.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about composition vs inheritance misuse
options: The Stack class extends ArrayList to reuse methods
The push and pop methods delegate to ArrayList methods
Inheriting from ArrayList exposes all public methods (add, remove, get) breaking the stack abstraction
questions.explanation: Extending ArrayList makes all its public methods available on Stack, including get(index), add(element), etc. This breaks the LIFO contract of a stack. Users can call stack.get(0) or stack.add(0, element). Fix: use composition (wrap an ArrayList as a private field) and expose only push/pop/peek.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about enum with methods and mutable state
options: The enum TrafficLight defines colors and behaviors
The getColor method returns the current color
Enum constants are effectively final but the instance field 'color' is mutable, allowing state changes across references
questions.explanation: While enum constants are singletons, their instance fields can be mutable. Fix: make fields final and remove the setter, or use an unmodifiable representation.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about incorrect this vs super in method overriding
options: The parent class has a greet method
The child class overrides greet correctly
Calling this.greet() inside the override causes infinite recursion instead of calling the parent
questions.explanation: Inside Child.greet(), calling greet() (or this.greet()) calls Child.greet() again, causing StackOverflowError. To call the parent's version, use super.greet(). Fix: replace greet() with super.greet() to invoke the parent implementation.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about record equals and custom logic
options: The Email record stores address and domain
Records auto-generate equals based on all components
The equals comparison is case-sensitive by default; 'Java@Mail.com' won't equal 'java@mail.com'
questions.explanation: Record equals compares all components using their equals methods. String.equals is case-sensitive. For email comparison, case-insensitive matching is usually expected. Fix: convert to lowercase before storing, or override equals to compare case-insensitively (though overriding record equals loses the compact benefit).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about sealed class with permits
options: The sealed interface Payment permits CreditCard and PayPal
CreditCard and PayPal are records implementing Payment
Sealed classes require all permitted subclasses to be known at compile time in the same module
questions.explanation: Sealed classes restrict which types can implement/extend them. All permitted types must be in the same module (or package). If you add a new implementation later, you must update the permits clause. This is intentional for type safety but can be a maintenance burden. Fix: ensure all implementations are in the same compilation unit.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about circular reference in equals
options: The Node class has a reference to another Node
The equals method checks for the same instance first
The equals method calls other.equals(this) without a termination condition, causing infinite recursion
questions.explanation: When comparing node1.equals(node2), it calls node2.equals(node1), which calls node1.equals(node2), creating infinite recursion and StackOverflowError. Fix: compare fields directly instead of delegating equality back to the other object.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about interface with static method
options: The Validator interface defines a validate method
The default validateEmail method provides a reusable implementation
Static methods in interfaces cannot be overridden; calling validator.validate() invokes the abstract method, not the static one
questions.explanation: Static methods in interfaces belong to the interface itself, not to instances. They cannot be overridden or called polymorphically. If you want instance behavior, use default methods or abstract methods. The static validateEmail can only be called as Validator.validateEmail().

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about toString in nested objects
options: The Order class has a list of OrderItem objects
Each OrderItem has a product name and price
The Order toString does not override toString, so it prints the default hash code
questions.explanation: Without overriding toString() in Order, printing an Order shows the default Object.toString() output (Order@hashcode). This is unhelpful for debugging. Additionally, OrderItem also needs a custom toString for meaningful output. Fix: override toString in both classes.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about ConcurrentModificationException
options: The ArrayList is initialized with elements
The for-each loop iterates over the list
Removing elements during for-each iteration causes ConcurrentModificationException
questions.explanation: For-each loops use an iterator internally. Modifying the list structure (add/remove) during iteration invalidates the iterator, causing ConcurrentModificationException. Fix: use Iterator.remove(), removeIf(), or stream filter.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about HashMap with mutable keys
options: The key is a StringBuilder object
The value is stored correctly
Mutating the key after put changes its hashCode, making the entry unretrievable
questions.explanation: HashMap uses hashCode to locate buckets. If you modify a key after insertion, its hashCode changes, so get() looks in a different bucket. The old entry becomes 'orphaned' — still in the map but unreachable. Fix: use immutable keys (String, Integer, or records).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about ArrayList.remove with int vs Object
options: The list contains integers 0 through 4
The remove method is called with value 1
remove(1) removes the element at index 1, not the element with value 1
questions.explanation: ArrayList has two remove methods: remove(int index) and remove(Object obj). When calling remove(1) on a List<Integer>, Java calls remove(int index) because 1 is an int. This removes the element at index 1 (value 1), not all elements with value 1. Fix: use remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) to remove by value.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about unmodifiable collection
options: The list is created as unmodifiable
The unmodifiable wrapper prevents add/remove operations
The underlying original list can still be modified, changing the unmodifiable view
questions.explanation: Collections.unmodifiableList creates a view, not a copy. If you still have a reference to the original list, you can modify it, and those changes are reflected in the unmodifiable view. Fix: use List.copyOf() (Java 10+) or wrap a new ArrayList copy.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about HashMap null key
options: The HashMap stores a null key with value "found"
The get call uses a null key
HashMap allows one null key, so this works; the bug is elsewhere
questions.explanation: HashMap does allow one null key, so map.get(null) returns "found". This code actually works correctly. The 'bug' is that TreeMap does NOT allow null keys and would throw NullPointerException. The lesson is understanding the difference between HashMap and TreeMap null handling.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about wrong hashCode implementation
options: The Person class has name and age fields
The equals method compares name and age
hashCode returns only name.hashCode(), so two People with same name but different ages collide in HashMap
questions.explanation: If hashCode only uses name, then Person("Alice", 25) and Person("Alice", 30) have the same hash and land in the same bucket. This degrades HashMap performance to O(n) per bucket. Fix: include all fields used in equals in hashCode: return Objects.hash(name, age).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about subList view vs copy
options: The subList creates a view of the original list
The subList is printed correctly
Modifying the original list after subList causes ConcurrentModificationException in the subList view
questions.explanation: subList returns a view backed by the original list. If you modify the original list (add/remove) after creating the subList, the view becomes invalid and throws ConcurrentModificationException when accessed. Fix: create a copy: new ArrayList<>(list.subList(2, 5)).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about iterator invalidation
options: The Iterator is obtained from the ArrayList
The loop processes each element correctly
Calling list.add() during iteration invalidates the iterator
questions.explanation: Using the ArrayList's add method during iterator iteration changes the modCount, causing the iterator to detect a concurrent modification. Fix: use iterator.add() to add during iteration, or collect elements to add and apply after iteration.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about equals/hashCode with collection field
options: The Team class has a name and set of members
equals() compares name and members
hashCode uses the mutable set directly, so if members is modified after insertion in HashSet, the entry is orphaned
questions.explanation: If the HashSet field used in hashCode is mutable and modified after the object is placed in a HashSet, the hashCode changes, making the entry unreachable. Fix: use Objects.hash(name, new ArrayList<>(members)) or make the collection immutable.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Arrays.asList vs List.of
options: The list is created from an array of strings
The list is used to add a new element
Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list backed by the array; add/remove throws UnsupportedOperationException
questions.explanation: Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list. You can set() existing elements (since they're backed by the array), but add() and remove() throw UnsupportedOperationException because they would change the array's size. Fix: use new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(...)) for a resizable list.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about removeIf with predicate
options: The list contains integer values
The removeIf method filters elements correctly
removeIf with n -> n == 1 removes the first occurrence only; if duplicates exist, only one is removed
questions.explanation: removeIf removes ALL elements matching the predicate, not just the first. This code works correctly — it removes all occurrences of 1. The 'bug' is a misconception: removeIf is safe for multiple matches. However, if you wanted to remove only the first, you'd need to use an iterator with break.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about WeakHashMap behavior
options: The WeakHashMap stores String keys with Integer values
The garbage collector can reclaim keys with no strong references
WeakHashMap entries are cleared when the key is garbage collected, but String literals are interned and never collected
questions.explanation: String literals are interned and held in the string pool (a strong reference), so they're never garbage collected. WeakHashMap entries with interned string keys persist indefinitely, defeating the purpose. Fix: use non-interned strings (new String("...")) or a different key type.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about HashMap thread-safety
options: The HashMap is shared between two threads
Each thread adds entries to the map
HashMap is not thread-safe; concurrent modifications can cause infinite loops in the internal bucket structure
questions.explanation: HashMap's internal linked list can form a cycle during concurrent resize operations (in Java 7; in Java 8+ it uses trees but still has data races). This can cause infinite loops in get() operations. Fix: use ConcurrentHashMap or Collections.synchronizedMap().

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about PriorityQueue ordering
options: The PriorityQueue stores strings
The poll method returns the smallest element
PriorityQueue with natural ordering puts smallest first; if you expect largest first, you need a reverse comparator
questions.explanation: PriorityQueue uses natural ordering (smallest first) by default. If you want largest-first (max-heap), pass Collections.reverseOrder() as the comparator. This code works correctly for min-heap, but the assumption about ordering may be wrong for the use case.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about EnumMap vs HashMap
options: The enum DayOfWeek has 7 values
The map stores tasks for each day
Using HashMap with enum keys is slower than EnumMap; EnumMap uses ordinal-based array indexing
questions.explanation: HashMap uses hash-based lookup with bucket arrays, while EnumMap uses an internal array indexed by enum ordinal. EnumMap is significantly faster and more memory-efficient for enum keys. This isn't a correctness bug but a performance issue. Fix: use EnumMap<DayOfWeek, String> for enum keys.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about null in TreeMap
options: The TreeMap stores string keys
The put method is called with a null key
TreeMap does not allow null keys; this throws NullPointerException
questions.explanation: TreeMap uses Comparator (or natural ordering) which calls compareTo(), and compareTo cannot handle null. Attempting to put a null key throws NullPointerException. HashMap allows one null key, but TreeMap does not. Fix: use HashMap for nullable keys, or ensure keys are never null.

map.put(null, 1); // NullPointerException!

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about computeIfAbsent
options: The map stores word counts
The computeIfAbsent creates a new list if the key is absent
The lambda modifies the map during computation, potentially causing ConcurrentModificationException
questions.explanation: If the mapping function modifies the map (e.g., puts another key), it can cause ConcurrentModificationException or infinite recursion. The mapping function should only compute the value for the current key. Fix: avoid map modifications inside computeIfAbsent lambdas.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Stack usage
options: The Stack is used to reverse a string
The push and pop operations are correct
Stack extends Vector which is synchronized, making it slower; use Deque interface with ArrayDeque instead
questions.explanation: java.util.Stack extends Vector, which is synchronized. This adds unnecessary overhead for single-threaded use. The Deque interface (implemented by ArrayDeque) is the recommended replacement for Stack. Fix: Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about autoboxing overhead in collections
options: The ArrayList stores Integer objects
The loop adds values 0 through 9999
Each primitive int is autoboxed to Integer, creating 10000 objects; use IntStream or int[] for performance
questions.explanation: Autoboxing converts each int to an Integer object, allocating heap memory for each. For large iterations, this creates significant GC pressure. Fix: use IntStream.range(0, 10000).boxed().collect() or int[] for primitive-only use cases.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about iterator invalidation with HashMap
options: The HashMap iterates over its entry set
The iterator processes each entry correctly
Using map.put() during iteration causes ConcurrentModificationException
questions.explanation: HashMap's iterator detects structural modifications (add/remove/put). Calling map.put() during iteration increases modCount, causing ConcurrentModificationException on the next hasNext/next call. Fix: use iterator.remove() or collect keys to modify after iteration.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Stream parallel processing
options: The stream processes a list of integers
The sum is computed in parallel
Parallel streams use a shared ForkJoinPool; side effects in forEach can cause thread-safety issues
questions.explanation: parallel().forEach() can execute elements in any order on any thread. If the lambda has side effects (like modifying external state), it causes race conditions. Fix: use parallel().reduce() or collect() which are designed for parallel-safe operations.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about synchronized collection wrapper
options: The list is wrapped with Collections.synchronizedList
The add and remove operations are thread-safe
Iteration must be manually synchronized; for-each loop is NOT thread-safe even with synchronized wrapper
questions.explanation: Collections.synchronizedList synchronizes individual operations but not iteration. A for-each loop calls hasNext/next without holding the lock, allowing concurrent modification. Fix: synchronize on the list: synchronized(list) { for (String s : list) { ... } }

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Deque as Queue
options: The ArrayDeque is used as a queue
offer adds to the tail, poll removes from the head
peek returns null when empty, but element() throws NoSuchElementException; using peek incorrectly hides errors
questions.explanation: peek() returns null when the queue is empty, which can mask errors if you expect an element. element() throws NoSuchElementException, making bugs more visible. The 'bug' is choosing the wrong method for your error-handling strategy. Fix: use element() if empty queue is an error condition.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about missing contains check before add
options: The Set stores unique strings
The add method returns false if already present
Adding duplicate strings to a HashSet wastes computation; check contains() first for performance-sensitive code
questions.explanation: HashSet.add() already handles duplicates — it returns false without adding. Fix: if (set.contains(name)) skip; else set.add(name).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Spliterator characteristics
options: The Spliterator is obtained from an ArrayList
The trySplit method creates sub-spliterators for parallel processing
Spliterator characteristics affect parallel stream performance; wrong characteristics cause inefficient splitting
questions.explanation: Spliterator characteristics (ORDERED, SIZED, etc.) guide the parallel stream framework. If characteristics are wrong or missing, the framework may not split efficiently. For ArrayList, Spliterator.spliterator() returns ORDERED|SIZED|SUBSIZED which is optimal. This is a design consideration, not always a bug.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about stream creation:
options: Line 1: The list creation is correct
Line 2: stream() creates a sequential stream from the list
Line 3: forEach accepts a Consumer so it consumes the stream - the stream cannot be reused after this
questions.explanation: Streams are single-use. After forEach executes, the stream is consumed and cannot be reused. If you call stream() again on the same list it creates a fresh stream, but reusing the same stream variable will throw IllegalStateException. In this code the forEach is fine, but the real bug is that this pattern tempts developers to reuse the stream. Here forEach is terminal, so the stream is consumed. The code compiles and runs but demonstrates a common misunderstanding.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about filter and map:

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about flatMap:

Line 3: flatMap expects Function<T, Stream<R>> but map expects Function<T, R> - using map here would produce Stream<List<Integer>> instead of Stream<Integer>
questions.explanation: The bug is that map is used instead of flatMap. map(List::stream) on Stream<List<Integer>> produces Stream<Stream<Integer>>, not Stream<Integer>. flatMap is needed to flatten nested streams into a single stream. The code uses map, which compiles but produces the wrong intermediate type and fails at collect.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about sorted and distinct:
options: Line 1: The list has duplicate elements
Line 2: sorted() sorts elements in natural order

Line 3: distinct() must come before sorted() to remove duplicates - but here sorted comes first which is fine, the real issue is that distinct uses equals/hashCode and the Student class does not override them

Two Student objects with the same name and grade will not be considered duplicates. The result will contain both 'Alice' entries. questions.text: Find the bug in this code about reduce:

questions.explanation: The reduce with identity '' and accumulator (a, b) -> a + ", " + b produces a leading comma: ', Alice, Bob, Charlie'. The identity '' is prepended to the first element. questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Collectors.groupingBy:

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Collectors.partitioningBy:
options: Line 1: The list of numbers is correct

Line 3: partitioningBy returns Map<Boolean, List<T>> which always has both keys true and false even if one group is empty
questions.explanation: The code is actually correct in behavior, but the bug is that the developer uses groupingBy instead of partitioningBy. groupingBy with a predicate returns Map<Boolean, List<T>> too, but partitioningBy is specifically designed for boolean predicates and guarantees both partitions exist. The real bug is using groupingBy with a boolean function when partitioningBy was intended - both compile but partitioningBy is semantically correct and guarantees both true/false keys.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Collectors.joining:
options: Line 1: The list of words is correct

Line 3: joining with delimiter works correctly for strings
questions.explanation: The code uses Collectors.joining() without any arguments, which concatenates all elements with no delimiter, no prefix, and no suffix. The result is 'HelloWorldFoo' instead of a comma-separated string. The developer likely intended Collectors.joining(", ") to get 'Hello, World, Foo'.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Optional misuse:
options: Line 1: Optional.ofNullable handles potential null correctly
Line 2: orElse returns the value or the default
Line 3: orElseThrow creates a new exception - this is correct but the bug is that get() was called on the Optional before, which throws NoSuchElementException if empty
questions.explanation: The bug is using Optional.get() without checking isPresent() first. If Optional.ofNullable(name) is empty (name is null), calling .get() throws NoSuchElementException. The correct approach is to use orElse("default"), orElseThrow(), or ifPresent(). The code mixes get() with orElse which is redundant and dangerous.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about lambda effectively final:
options: Line 1: The variable count is declared as int
Line 2: The lambda captures count
Line 3: Modifying count inside the lambda body violates effectively final rule - lambdas can only capture effectively final variables
questions.explanation: The variable count is modified inside the lambda body (count++), which violates the effectively final requirement. Local variables referenced from a lambda must be effectively final - they cannot be modified after initialization. This causes a compilation error. Fix: use AtomicInteger or an array wrapper.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about peek vs forEach side effects:
options: Line 1: peek is used for debugging intermediate operations
Line 2: forEach is a terminal operation that consumes the stream
Line 3: peek should only be used for side effects like debugging, not for filtering - here peek performs filtering which is incorrect usage
questions.explanation: The bug is using peek() to filter elements. peek() is designed for debugging/observing stream elements, not for modifying them or performing filtering logic. The filtering should be done with filter(). Using peek() for logic that affects the stream's behavior is a misuse and makes the code confusing and potentially unreliable with lazy evaluation.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about findFirst and anyMatch:
options: Line 1: The list of numbers is correct
Line 2: findFirst returns Optional<Integer> which is correct
Line 3: anyMatch returns boolean - using it to check existence then filter+findFirst is redundant and inefficient
questions.explanation: The code calls anyMatch to check if an element exists, then calls filter+findFirst to get it. questions.text: Find the bug in this code about parallelStream with non-thread-safe collection:
options: Line 1: parallelStream() creates a parallel stream
Line 2: filter and map are applied in parallel
Line 3: collect(Collectors.toList()) is not thread-safe with parallelStream - ArrayList is not thread-safe and may lose elements or throw ConcurrentModificationException
questions.explanation: Using collect(Collectors.toList()) with parallelStream is unsafe because ArrayList is not thread-safe. Multiple threads may try to add elements concurrently, causing data loss or ConcurrentModificationException. Fix: use collect(Collectors.toConcurrentMap(...)) or collect with toList() which is thread-safe in Java 16+, or use a concurrent collection.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about wrong flatMap usage:
options: Line 1: The list of sentences is correct
Line 2: split(" ") splits each sentence into words
Line 3: flatMap expects Function<T, Stream<R>> but Arrays.stream returns Stream<String[]> which is wrong - should use Arrays.stream(words) or Pattern.compile("\\s+").splitAsStream(sentence)
questions.explanation: The bug is that sentence.split(" ") returns String[], and flatMap expects a function that returns a Stream. Arrays.stream(sentence.split(" ")) is correct, but the code uses map(Arrays::stream) which would produce Stream<Stream<String>> from flatMap's perspective. The correct usage is flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.split(" "))).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about missing terminal operation:
options: Line 1: The list creation is correct
Line 2: filter creates an intermediate stream
Line 3: map creates another intermediate stream - without a terminal operation like collect, forEach, or count, nothing executes
questions.explanation: The stream pipeline has no terminal operation. filter() and map() are intermediate operations that are lazy - they build a pipeline but don't process anything until a terminal operation is invoked. The result variable receives an unevaluated stream pipeline, not the processed list. Fix: add .collect(Collectors.toList()) at the end.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about wrong reduce identity:
options: Line 1: The list of strings is correct
Line 2: reduce with identity "" starts concatenation from empty string
Line 3: The identity value is type String but the operation produces a comma-separated string - the identity "" with separator causes leading comma ', Alice, Bob, Charlie'
questions.explanation: Using reduce("", (a,b) -> a + ", " + b) produces ', Alice, Bob, Charlie' because the empty string identity is prepended. The reduce operation combines the identity with the first element, producing an unwanted leading comma. Fix: use Collectors.joining(", ") or a custom reducer that checks if 'a' is empty before appending.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about side effects in parallelStream:
options: Line 1: parallelStream() processes elements in parallel
Line 2: filter and map are applied correctly
Line 3: Using a non-atomic counter with parallelStream causes race conditions - count++ is not atomic and loses increments
questions.explanation: The code uses a plain int counter (count++) inside a parallelStream pipeline via peek(). In parallel execution, multiple threads read-modify-write the counter simultaneously, losing increments due to race conditions. Fix: use AtomicInteger with getAndIncrement(), or better, avoid side effects in streams entirely and use count() terminal operation.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about wrong collector usage:
options: Line 1: The list of numbers is correct
Line 2: groupingBy groups numbers into even/odd
Line 3: counting() returns Long but the map values are List<Integer> - type mismatch between groupingBy key type and downstream collector
questions.explanation: The code uses Collectors.groupingBy with a classifier that returns Boolean and a downstream collector of counting(). This produces Map<Boolean, Long>, but the variable is declared as Map<Boolean, List<Integer>>. The types are incompatible. Fix: either use Collectors.toList() as downstream, or change the variable type to Map<Boolean, Long>.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about flatMap vs map confusion:
options: Line 1: The Optional contains a list of strings
Line 2: map would wrap the result in another Optional
Line 3: flatMap flattens Optional<Optional<List<String>>> to Optional<List<String>> - using map here produces nested Optional
questions.explanation: When you have Optional<List<String>> and use map(x -> x.stream()), you get Optional<Stream<String>>. But flatMap(x -> x.stream()) correctly produces Stream<String>. The code uses map which wraps the stream in an extra Optional layer. The bug is that map is used instead of flatMap, producing the wrong type.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about takeWhile/dropWhile:
options: Line 1: The list is unsorted
Line 2: takeWhile stops at the first element that doesn't match the predicate
Line 3: takeWhile/dropWhile require a sorted stream or the behavior is undefined for unsorted input - elements may be skipped unexpectedly
questions.explanation: takeWhile and dropWhile are designed for ordered streams. For unordered streams, they stop processing at ANY element that doesn't match the predicate, not necessarily the first one in sequence. With an unsorted list like [3, 1, 4, 1, 5], takeWhile(n -> n < 3) might return empty or [3] depending on encounter order. Fix: sort the stream first or use filter.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Stream.ofNullable:
options: Line 1: Stream.ofNullable creates a stream with one element if non-null, or empty if null
Line 2: flatMap is used to flatten the stream of streams
Line 3: Stream.ofNullable(null).flatMap(...) returns an empty stream, so the final result is empty when name is null
questions.explanation: The bug is that Stream.ofNullable(name) when name is null produces an empty stream. flatMap on an empty stream produces an empty stream. The code does not handle the case where name is null properly - it silently produces no output instead of providing a default value. The developer likely intended to use Optional.ofNullable(name).stream() or Stream.ofNullable(name).findFirst().orElse("default").

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Stream.toList() vs collect(toList()):
options: Line 1: Stream.toList() is a convenient terminal operation in Java 16+
Line 2: collect(Collectors.toList()) returns a mutable ArrayList
Line 3: Stream.toList() returns an unmodifiable list - attempting to add elements throws UnsupportedOperationException
questions.explanation: The code calls stream().toList() which returns an unmodifiable list in Java 16+. Then it tries to add an element with .add(), which throws UnsupportedOperationException. If a mutable list is needed, use .collect(Collectors.toList()) instead. The toList() method is for cases where an unmodifiable snapshot is acceptable.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about sorted performance with large streams:
options: Line 1: parallelStream() is used for performance
Line 2: sorted() is called on the parallel stream

Line 3: sorted() on a parallel stream forces the entire stream to be processed before any elements are emitted - this defeats the purpose of parallel processing for large datasets and uses O(n) additional memory
questions.explanation: sorted() is a stateful operation that must see all elements before it can sort them. On a parallel stream, this forces synchronization barriers and buffers all elements, negating much of the parallel advantage. For large datasets, this can cause significant memory overhead. Consider whether sorting is truly needed or if a different approach (like min/max) would suffice.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about null elements in streams:
options: Line 1: The list contains null elements
Line 2: filter and map are chained correctly
