This is a common leak in application servers that redeploy applications. Fix: ensure all class instances are GC'd before closing the classloader.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about wrong class in equals():
options: Line 1: equals() compares this with obj
Line 2: getClass() is used instead of instanceof
Line 3: Using getClass() instead of instanceof breaks the symmetry contract - subclasses are not equal to parent classes even if fields match, violating the equals contract
questions.explanation: Using getClass() in equals() breaks the symmetry contract. If B extends A and both have the same fields, a.equals(b) returns false (because b.getClass() is B, not A) but b.equals(a) might return true (if B's equals uses instanceof A). Fix: use instanceof for the type check, or ensure the class is final.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about circular dependency:
options: ServiceA correctly injects ServiceB
ServiceB correctly injects ServiceA
Circular dependency between ServiceA and ServiceB causes Spring to fail at startup
questions.explanation: ServiceA depends on ServiceB and ServiceB depends on ServiceA, creating a circular dependency. Spring cannot resolve this at startup and throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. Fix: use @Lazy on one injection point, extract a shared interface, or restructure the design to break the cycle.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about bean scope:
options: The repository is correctly defined as @Repository
The service uses constructor injection properly
UserService is singleton but holds mutable state (list of users) shared across all requests
questions.explanation: UserService is a singleton (default scope) but maintains a mutable List<User>. All requests share the same instance, so concurrent requests will see and modify the same list, causing data corruption and race conditions. Fix: remove mutable state or use request/session scope.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Spring Boot autoconfiguration:
options: The @SpringBootApplication annotation is correctly placed on the main class
The @ComponentScan annotation explicitly scans the correct packages
CustomDataSourceConfig is missing @Configuration, so Spring Boot ignores it and uses the auto-configured DataSource
questions.explanation: CustomDataSourceConfig is not annotated with @Configuration (or @Component), so Spring does not recognize it as a configuration class. Spring Boot will use its default auto-configured DataSource instead. Fix: add @Configuration to the class.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @Autowired field injection:
options: The OrderService class is correctly annotated as @Service
The repository is correctly annotated as @Repository
Field injection with @Autowired makes the dependency hidden and prevents unit testing without Spring context
questions.explanation: Field injection via @Autowired hides dependencies, makes the class tightly coupled to Spring, and prevents instantiation without the Spring context (or reflection hacks like @InjectMocks). Constructor injection is preferred because it makes dependencies explicit, allows immutability, and enables easy unit testing.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @Configuration and @Bean:
options: The @Configuration annotation is correctly applied
The @Bean methods return the correct types
Calling another @Bean method directly within @Configuration causes a different instance instead of the proxied bean
questions.explanation: In a @Configuration class, calling another @Bean method directly (e.g., dataSource()) bypasses the CGLIB proxy that Spring creates. This means you get a NEW instance instead of the managed singleton bean. Fix: inject the dependency via method parameters.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @Value property injection:
options: The @Value annotation uses the correct SpEL syntax
The property key matches application.properties
Missing default value causes startup failure when app.port is not defined
questions.explanation: The @Value("${app.port}") expression does not provide a default value. If the property is not defined, Spring throws IllegalArgumentException at startup. Fix: use @Value("${app.port:8080}") to provide a default.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @Profile:
options: The dev profile is correctly activated via @Profile
The prod profile bean is correctly defined
Both beans have @Profile("dev"), causing NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException when dev profile is active
questions.explanation: Both DataSource beans are annotated with @Profile("dev"), so when the dev profile is active, Spring finds two qualifying DataSource beans and cannot decide which to inject. Fix: give each bean a distinct profile.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @Transactional:
options: The @Transactional annotation is correctly placed on the public method
The saveAll call is properly within the transaction
Calling the private method directly bypasses the proxy, so @Transactional on the private method has no effect
questions.explanation: Spring uses AOP proxies to implement @Transactional. Private methods cannot be intercepted by proxies, so @Transactional on a private method does nothing. Fix: move @Transactional to the public method or extract the method to another bean.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @RestController and @RequestBody:
options: The @RestController annotation is correctly applied
The @RequestMapping maps to the correct HTTP method
Missing @RequestBody annotation means Spring treats the parameter as query params, not JSON deserialization
questions.explanation: The createUser method receives CreateUserRequest without @RequestBody. Without it, Spring treats it as query parameter binding, not JSON deserialization. Fix: add @RequestBody to the parameter.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about REST API design:
options: The GET method correctly retrieves a resource
The DELETE method correctly removes a resource
Using PUT for partial update violates REST conventions; PATCH should be used for partial updates
questions.explanation: PUT is defined as a full replacement of the resource. Using it for a partial update violates REST semantics. PATCH should be used for partial updates. Fix: use @PatchMapping.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @Transactional exception handling:
options: The @Transactional annotation is correctly applied to the method
The try-catch block handles the exception gracefully
Catching the exception prevents Spring from seeing it, so the transaction commits instead of rolling back
questions.explanation: By default, Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions. If you catch the exception inside the method, Spring never sees it and the transaction commits. Fix: rethrow the exception or use TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly().

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about transaction propagation:
options: The outer method starts a transaction correctly with @Transactional
The inner method saves the order to the database
Inner method with REQUIRES_NEW runs in a separate transaction, so if outer rolls back, the inner data persists inconsistently
questions.explanation: When innerMethod uses REQUIRES_NEW, it suspends the outer transaction and starts a new one. If the outer method throws an exception and rolls back, the inner transaction has already committed, causing inconsistent data. Fix: use REQUIRED (default) or handle the commit/rollback logic explicitly.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about missing @Transactional rollback for checked exceptions:
options: The @Transactional annotation is correctly applied
The method throws a checked exception as expected
Spring only rolls back on unchecked exceptions by default; checked exceptions cause the transaction to commit
questions.explanation: By default, @Transactional only rolls back on RuntimeException and Error. Checked exceptions like IOException do not trigger rollback. Fix: use @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @Conditional bean registration:
options: The @ConditionalOnProperty annotation correctly checks the config property
The CacheConfig class is properly annotated as @Configuration
Both cache beans have the same @ConditionalOnProperty without havingValue, causing ambiguity when the property is set
questions.explanation: @ConditionalOnProperty(name="cache.type") only checks existence, not value. When cache.type is set, both beans qualify and Spring cannot decide which to create. Fix: add havingValue to each condition to make them mutually exclusive.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about lazy initialization:
options: The @Lazy annotation correctly defers bean creation
The eager bean is created at startup as expected
Lazy bean injected into a singleton may cause issues if accessed before the context fully initializes
questions.explanation: When @Lazy is on the injection point, Spring injects a proxy. The actual bean is created on first method call. If the lazy bean's own dependencies are not ready at that point, or if accessed during context initialization, it can fail unexpectedly.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @ComponentScan:
options: The main application class is in the correct base package
The @ComponentScan annotation scans the correct packages
ComponentScan only scans its own package and sub-packages, so controllers in com.other.app are never discovered
questions.explanation: @SpringBootApplication on com.example.app only scans com.example.app and sub-packages. If controllers are in com.other.app, they will not be found. Fix: specify @ComponentScan("com.other.app") or restructure packages.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @MockBean in tests:
options: The @SpringBootTest annotation loads the full application context
The @MockBean annotation correctly replaces the real UserService bean
Using @SpringBootTest loads the full context when only the controller layer is needed, slowing tests unnecessarily
questions.explanation: @SpringBootTest loads the full application context including all beans, databases, and external services. For testing only a REST controller, @WebMvcTest should be used instead. Fix: replace @SpringBootTest with @WebMvcTest(UserController.class).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about proxy vs target in Spring AOP:
options: The @Transactional annotation on the public method is correctly applied
The AuditAspect correctly intercepts calls to the service
Internal method calls within the same bean bypass the AOP proxy, so @Transactional on the callee has no effect
questions.explanation: Spring AOP uses proxies. When methodA() calls methodB() within the same bean, the call goes directly to methodB() without going through the proxy. If methodB() has @Transactional, it will not take effect. This is the self-invocation problem.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about missing validation annotations:
options: The @Valid annotation triggers validation on the request body
The @RequestBody correctly deserializes the JSON payload
The User class is missing validation annotations on its fields, so validation never occurs
questions.explanation: Even with @Valid on the controller parameter, the User DTO fields have no validation annotations (@NotBlank, @Size, etc.). Spring validation has nothing to validate. Fix: add Jakarta Bean Validation annotations to the fields.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @RequestMapping method mismatch:
options: The path /api/orders is correctly mapped
The method returns a valid ResponseEntity
@GetMapping used for a mutation operation violates REST semantics and fails if client sends POST
questions.explanation: createOrder performs a mutation but is mapped with @GetMapping. GET should be safe and idempotent. A client sending POST gets 405 Method Not Allowed. Fix: use @PostMapping.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about bean override:
options: The first DataSource bean is correctly defined
The @Primary annotation marks the preferred bean
Spring Boot allows bean definition overriding by default, so the second bean silently replaces the first
questions.explanation: By default, Spring Boot allows bean definition overriding. When two beans of the same type exist, the last one wins. h2DataSource silently replaces myDataSource. Fix: set spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=false or use @Primary.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about application.properties placeholders:
options: The database URL property is correctly defined
The pool size property uses valid integer type
The placeholder ${db.url} uses a dot which Spring interprets as a nested property, causing binding ambiguity
questions.explanation: Spring property placeholders use dots as nested property separators. ${db.url} can cause ambiguous binding. Fix: use underscores (db_url) or ensure consistent naming conventions.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @PathVariable:
options: The @RequestBody correctly binds the JSON payload
The @RequestParam correctly binds the query parameter
The path variable {id} is missing @PathVariable, so Spring will not bind it from the URL
questions.explanation: The method maps /api/orders/{id}/items but the id parameter has no @PathVariable. Spring will not bind the URL path segment to the parameter. Fix: add @PathVariable.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @ConfigurationProperties binding:
options: The @ConfigurationProperties annotation correctly specifies the prefix
The @EnableConfigurationProperties annotation registers the class
The fields use primitive int and boolean without defaults, causing startup failure if properties are missing
questions.explanation: The poolSize and useSsl fields are primitives. If properties are not set, Spring cannot assign a default. Fix: use wrapper types (Integer, Boolean) or provide defaults in application.properties.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @MockBean and test isolation:
options: The @WebMvcTest annotation correctly loads only the web layer
The MockMvc is correctly injected
@MockBean stubs the service but the test only checks HTTP status, never verifying the controller calls the service correctly
questions.explanation: @WebMvcTest does not load @Service beans, so @MockBean is needed. However, mocking means the test never verifies the controller correctly calls the service. The test only checks HTTP semantics. Fix: add verify() calls or accept the trade-off.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about JUnit 5 @BeforeEach:
options: The @BeforeEach annotation correctly marks the setup method
The @Test annotation is correctly applied
@BeforeEach adds to a shared list instead of creating a fresh instance, causing test pollution
questions.explanation: The list is initialized once at field declaration. @BeforeEach adds items to the existing list instead of creating a new one. After test1 adds an item, test2 sees the modified list. Fix: reinitialize the list in @BeforeEach.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about JUnit 5 assertions:
options: The assertEquals checks the correct expected value
The method under test returns the correct result
Asserting (actual, expected) reverses the convention, causing confusing failure messages
questions.explanation: JUnit assertions follow (expected, actual) convention. The code has assertEquals(result, 5), reversing the order. Fix: use assertEquals(5, result).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Mockito mock vs spy:
options: The mock of UserService correctly stubs the findById method
The verify call checks that save was invoked
Using spy on a real object means save() actually executes, causing side effects in the test
questions.explanation: A spy wraps a real object. When save() is called on the spy, the real method executes. Fix: use a mock instead or stub the save() method on the spy.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about verify in Mockito:
options: The mock is correctly configured to return a value
The test method is correctly annotated with @Test
verify(never()) is called on a mock that was never injected into the service
questions.explanation: The test calls verify(never()) on a local mock that was never injected into the service. The service uses a real EmailService instance. Fix: inject the mock into the service.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @ParameterizedTest:
options: The @ParameterizedTest annotation is correctly used
The @ValueSource provides valid string arguments
The assertion checks length > 5 but the parameterized values include strings with length <= 5
questions.explanation: The test asserts length > 5 but @ValueSource includes "abc" (length 3). Fix: adjust the assertion or remove values that fail the condition.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about exception testing:
options: The @Test annotation is correctly applied
The method under test correctly throws an exception
assertThrows catches the wrong exception type, so different exceptions cause unexpected test failures
questions.explanation: The test expects NumberFormatException but the method may throw IllegalArgumentException. If a different exception is thrown, the test fails unexpectedly. Fix: catch the correct exception type.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @Nested test classes:
options: The @Nested annotation correctly groups related tests
The outer class setup runs before all nested tests
The inner @BeforeEach runs in addition to the outer one, potentially causing double initialization
questions.explanation: @BeforeEach in nested classes runs in addition to the outer @BeforeEach. The outer creates a stack, then the inner pushes items. While this works here, the pattern is fragile and can cause unexpected double initialization.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Mockito @ExtendWith:
options: The MockitoExtension correctly initializes mocks
The @BeforeEach sets up test data properly
Using @ExtendWith but creating the service with new bypasses mock injection
questions.explanation: @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) initializes @Mock fields, but if the service creates its own dependencies internally, the mock is never injected. Fix: pass the mock via constructor.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about argument captors:
options: The @Captor annotation is correctly declared
The verify call captures the argument correctly
ArgumentCaptor.capture() is called outside verify(), so it does not actually capture anything
questions.explanation: capture() must be called inside verify(). Calling it outside means no argument is captured, and getValue() throws an illegal state exception. Fix: place capture() inside verify().

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about mock not stubbed:
options: The @Mock annotation correctly creates a mock
The service under test is properly instantiated
Calling a method on a mock without stubbing returns null, causing NullPointerException
questions.explanation: A Mockito mock returns null for unstubbed methods. If the service calls repo.findById() and uses the result without null check, NPE occurs. Fix: stub the method with when().thenReturn().

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about test interdependence:
options: Each test method is independent and can run in any order
The @BeforeEach method creates a fresh service for each test
Tests depend on execution order: test2 relies on state modified by test1
questions.explanation: test2 asserts count == 2, depending on test1 having incremented. JUnit does not guarantee execution order. Fix: each test should set up its own state.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about assertion message parameter:
options: The assertEquals checks the correct values
The test method is correctly annotated
The assertion message is placed as the last parameter which JUnit interprets as the actual value
questions.explanation: JUnit 5 assertEquals expects (expected, actual, message). The code correctly places the message last, but the issue is that the message string is treated as a third parameter. Fix: ensure (expected, actual, message) ordering.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @CsvSource parameterized test:
options: The @ParameterizedTest annotation is correctly used
The @CsvSource provides the test data
The CSV values have incorrect quoting, causing null to be parsed as a String instead of actual null
questions.explanation: In @CsvSource, unquoted null is treated as the String "null". The test expects null input but receives the literal string. Fix: use @NullSource for null values or configure nullValues.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about flaky test with time dependency:
options: The test correctly verifies the retry logic
The mock stubbing returns the expected values
The test uses real Thread.sleep and timing assertions, making it flaky on slow machines
questions.explanation: The test asserts elapsed time between 2000-3000ms. On a slow CI machine, Thread.sleep overhead can exceed 3000ms. Fix: use a Clock abstraction and mock it.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about missing edge cases:
options: The test correctly verifies the normal case
The mock is properly configured
The test only covers the happy path, missing null input, empty list, and boundary values
questions.explanation: The test only verifies sum for a valid list. It does not test empty list, null list, single element, or Integer.MAX_VALUE overflow. Fix: add tests for edge cases.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @BeforeAll and @AfterAll:
options: @BeforeAll correctly runs once before all tests
@AfterAll correctly runs once after all tests
The instance method is annotated with @BeforeAll but it must be static
questions.explanation: @BeforeAll and @AfterAll methods must be static by default. If not static and the class does not use @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS), JUnit throws a validation error. Fix: make the method static.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @SpringBootTest loading full context:
options: The test class is annotated with @SpringBootTest
The @Autowired repository is correctly injected
Using @SpringBootTest loads the entire application context, making the test slow and dependent on external services
questions.explanation: @SpringBootTest loads the full Spring context. If the database is unavailable, the test fails. Fix: use @DataJpaTest for repository tests or mock external dependencies.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Mockito spy stubbing:
options: The spy correctly wraps the real object
The test method is annotated with @Test
Stubbing doReturn on a spy with when() causes the real method to execute before the stub takes effect
questions.explanation: when(spy.method()) on a spy causes the real method to execute first (to get the argument), then the stub overrides the return value. For void methods, this causes side effects. Fix: use doReturn().when(spy).method().

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Jacoco coverage gap:
options: The test covers the calculateDiscount method
The test verifies the result is correct
The test only covers the if branch; the else branch (no discount) is never tested
questions.explanation: The test only calls calculateDiscount(150), taking the if branch. The else branch (amount < 100) is never exercised. Fix: add a test case with amount < 100.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about TDD cycle violation:
options: The test is written before the implementation
The test correctly describes the expected behavior
Writing the test after the implementation violates TDD red-green-refactor
questions.explanation: In TDD, you write a failing test first (red), then implement (green), then refactor. Writing implementation first leads to tests that confirm existing behavior rather than specifying requirements.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about MockMvc status assertion:
options: The @WebMvcTest loads the controller correctly
The @MockBean stubs the service dependency
perform() is called but no andExpect() is chained, so no assertion is made on the response
questions.explanation: The test calls mockMvc.perform() but does not chain andExpect(). The request executes but no verification occurs. Fix: chain .andExpect(status().isOk()).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about test coverage of exception path:
options: The test verifies the happy path correctly
The mock is properly configured
The test does not cover the exception path when repository.save() throws
questions.explanation: The test only covers successful save. If repository.save() throws, behavior is untested. Fix: add a test that stubs the mock to throw and verifies the service handles it.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about test reset between tests:
options: The @BeforeEach creates a fresh service instance
The mock is correctly annotated with @Mock
Without @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), @Mock fields remain null
questions.explanation: Without @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) or MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(), @Mock fields are never initialized. Fix: add @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to the class.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @MethodSource parameterized test:
options: The @MethodSource annotation references the correct method
The test method parameters match the stream types
The provider method is not static, so JUnit cannot invoke it
questions.explanation: @MethodSource requires the provider method to be static (unless using @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)). The method testCases() is an instance method. Fix: make it static.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about @DisplayName missing on nested class:
options: The @DisplayName on the method provides a readable description
The test method is correctly annotated with @Test
The @Nested class lacks @DisplayName, making test reports harder to navigate
questions.explanation: While not a functional bug, the @Nested class lacks @DisplayName. Test output shows generic class names instead of descriptive labels. Fix: add @DisplayName to nested classes for clearer reports.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Singleton pattern:
options: The enum singleton is thread-safe and serialization-safe
The getInstance() method returns the single instance
The static field is not volatile or synchronized, so multiple threads can create separate instances
questions.explanation: Without synchronization or volatile, two threads can simultaneously check instance == null and both create a new instance. Fix: use enum singleton, double-checked locking with volatile, or eager initialization.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Factory Method pattern:
options: The factory method creates the correct object type
The factory method is correctly abstract
The factory returns a concrete type instead of an interface, preventing polymorphism
questions.explanation: The factory method returns the concrete Car type instead of a Vehicle interface. This couples the client to the implementation. Fix: return Vehicle from the factory method.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Builder pattern:
options: The builder correctly sets each field
The build() method returns the constructed object
The builder has no validation, so invalid objects can be constructed (e.g., negative price)
questions.explanation: The builder allows constructing a Product with negative price or null name. The build() method should validate fields. Fix: add validation in build().

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Prototype pattern:
options: The clone() method is correctly overridden
The prototype creates a copy of the object
Shallow copy of the tags list means both original and clone share the same list
questions.explanation: Object.clone() performs a shallow copy. The tags list is a reference type, so the clone shares the same ArrayList instance. Adding a tag to the clone also adds it to the original. Fix: perform a deep copy of the list in clone().

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Adapter pattern:
options: The adapter wraps the legacy system correctly
The adapter implements the modern interface
The adapter delegates to the wrong method of the adaptee, returning incorrect data
questions.explanation: The adapter's getName() calls adaptee.getFullLabel() which returns the full label (e.g., 'John Doe - Admin') instead of just the name. Fix: call the correct method or parse the result.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Decorator pattern:
options: The decorator correctly wraps the base component
The decorator implements the same interface as the base component
The decorator does not delegate the core method to the wrapped component
questions.explanation: The LoggingDecorator overrides getPrice() but does not call wrapped.getPrice(), instead returning a hardcoded value. A decorator should add behavior while delegating the core operation. Fix: call wrapped.getPrice() and add logging around it.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Proxy pattern:
options: The proxy implements the same interface as the real subject
The proxy correctly delays creation of the real subject
The proxy forwards the call to the real subject but does not check authorization before forwarding
questions.explanation: The proxy's method delegates to realSubject without checking the user's permissions first. A protection proxy should verify authorization before forwarding. Fix: add the authorization check before the delegation.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Facade pattern:
options: The facade provides a simplified interface to the complex subsystem
The facade correctly delegates to subsystem components
The facade exposes internal subsystem objects, breaking encapsulation
questions.explanation: The facade's getInventory() method returns the internal Map directly, allowing external code to modify it. A facade should return a copy or an unmodifiable view. Fix: return Collections.unmodifiableMap(inventory).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Command pattern:
options: The command encapsulates the action and receiver
The invoker correctly stores and executes commands
The command does not implement undo, so the system cannot roll back executed operations
questions.explanation: The Command pattern typically requires both execute() and undo() methods. Without undo(), the system cannot reverse operations. Fix: add an undo() method to the Command interface and implement it in concrete commands.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Observer pattern:
options: The subject correctly maintains a list of observers
Observers are correctly notified when state changes
Observers are never removed from the list, causing memory leaks
questions.explanation: The subject adds observers but never removes them. If observers are registered but not unregistered, the subject holds strong references to them, preventing garbage collection. Fix: add a detach() method.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Strategy pattern:
options: The strategy interface defines a common algorithm
The context correctly delegates to the strategy
The context does not check for null strategy, causing NullPointerException at runtime
questions.explanation: If no strategy is set (null), calling strategy.execute() throws NPE. The context should validate that a strategy is assigned before executing. Fix: add a null check or require strategy in the constructor.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Template Method pattern:
options: The abstract class defines the template method correctly
Subclasses override the abstract steps as required
The constructor calls an overridable method, which may execute before the subclass is fully initialized
questions.explanation: If the template method or any overridable method is called from the constructor, the subclass's fields may not be initialized yet. This is a common pitfall in Java. Fix: do not call overridable methods from constructors.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about State pattern:
options: The state interface defines the common operations
The context correctly delegates to the current state
State transitions are not handled correctly, causing the machine to get stuck in an invalid state
questions.explanation: The VendingState interface has processPayment() and dispenseItem(), but the IdleState transitions to DispensingState without setting the next valid state. The machine gets stuck. Fix: ensure each state sets the next state correctly.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Chain of Responsibility:
options: Each handler has a reference to the next handler
The chain correctly passes the request along
The chain has no termination condition, causing infinite loops when no handler processes the request
questions.explanation: If no handler in the chain can process the request and the last handler calls next.handle(), it creates an infinite loop (or NPE if next is null). Fix: add a null check for next and a terminal handler.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Mediator pattern:
options: The mediator coordinates communication between components
Components communicate through the mediator
Components directly reference each other instead of going through the mediator
questions.explanation: The ChatRoom mediator is used, but the User class also holds direct references to other users. This breaks the mediator pattern because components bypass the mediator. Fix: all communication should go through the mediator.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Visitor pattern:
options: The visitor interface defines visit methods for each element type
The elements correctly accept the visitor
Adding a new element type requires modifying the visitor interface, violating the open/closed principle
questions.explanation: The Visitor pattern's strength is adding new operations without changing elements. However, adding a new element type (e.g., VideoFile) requires adding a new visit method to the visitor interface and all implementations. This is a known limitation. Fix: consider default methods in the visitor interface (Java 8+).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Flyweight pattern:
options: The flyweight factory caches shared objects
The factory correctly returns cached instances for the same key
The factory creates a new object every time instead of checking the cache first
questions.explanation: The factory's getFont() method creates a new Font every time without checking if one with the same key already exists. This defeats the purpose of the Flyweight pattern. Fix: check the cache before creating a new instance.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Bridge pattern:
options: The abstraction holds a reference to the implementation
The abstraction delegates work to the implementation
The abstraction and implementation are tightly coupled, defeating the purpose of the pattern
questions.explanation: The RemoteControl abstraction creates the Device implementation in its constructor (new TV()). This tight coupling means you cannot switch implementations at runtime. Fix: accept the implementation via constructor injection.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Composite pattern:
options: The component interface defines common operations
The composite correctly manages child components
The leaf component throws UnsupportedOperationException for add/remove, but the client does not check the type
questions.explanation: The Leaf class throws UnsupportedOperationException for add()/remove(). If the client calls these on a leaf without checking, it crashes at runtime. Fix: either return false/null for unsupported operations or use a type check before calling.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about SOLID - Single Responsibility:
options: The class has a single, well-defined responsibility
The method correctly implements the business logic
The class handles both business logic and persistence, violating the Single Responsibility Principle
questions.explanation: The UserService class both manages user business logic and performs database operations directly. This violates SRP because it has two reasons to change: business rules and persistence. Fix: extract persistence to a separate repository class.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about SOLID - Open/Closed Principle:
options: The class is open for extension
The class is closed for modification
Adding a new discount type requires modifying the existing DiscountCalculator class
questions.explanation: The DiscountCalculator uses if/else to check discount type. Adding a new discount type (e.g., BogoDiscount) requires modifying this class, violating OCP. Fix: use the Strategy pattern or polymorphism to make it open for extension.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about SOLID - Liskov Substitution Principle:
options: The subclass correctly extends the base class
The subclass overrides the method with compatible behavior
The subclass changes the method's contract, so substituting it for the parent causes unexpected behavior
questions.explanation: Square changes the behavior of setWidth() to also change height, violating the expectation that width and height are independent. When a Square is substituted for a Rectangle, calculations break. Fix: do not make Square a subtype of Rectangle, or use separate interfaces.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about SOLID - Interface Segregation:
options: The interface defines a focused set of methods
The implementation class correctly implements all methods
The interface forces implementors to provide methods they may not need
questions.explanation: Workable forces all implementors to provide eat() and sleep(). A Robot class implementing Workable would need to provide eat() and sleep() which make no sense. Fix: split into smaller interfaces (Workable, Eatable, Sleepable).

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about SOLID - Dependency Inversion:
options: The high-level module depends on an abstraction
The low-level module implements the abstraction
The high-level module directly depends on a low-level module instead of an abstraction
questions.explanation: OrderService directly depends on MySQLDatabase (low-level), making it hard to test or switch databases. Fix: introduce a Database interface and inject it via constructor.

questions.text: Find the bug in this code about Builder pattern missing step validation:
options: The builder correctly accumulates all required fields
The build() method returns the constructed object
The build() method does not validate that all required fields are set, allowing incomplete objects
questions.explanation: The builder allows calling build() without setting required fields like name or email. The resulting object will have null values that may cause NPE later. Fix: validate required fields in build() and throw IllegalStateException if missing.

questions.text: Find the bug in this SQL injection vulnerable code:
options: The Connection is obtained from DriverManager correctly
The ResultSet is iterated properly
The query string is built with string concatenation from user input
questions.explanation: Building SQL queries with string concatenation using user input allows SQL injection attacks. An attacker could enter ' OR '1'='1 to bypass authentication. Always use PreparedStatement with parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection.

questions.text: Find the bug in this JDBC resource handling code:
options: The PreparedStatement is created correctly
The ResultSet processing logic is correct
Resources are not closed in a finally block or try-with-resources, causing connection leaks
questions.explanation: When an exception occurs after obtaining the Connection but before reaching the close statements, the resources are never closed. This causes connection leaks that will eventually exhaust the connection pool. Use try-with-resources to guarantee cleanup.

questions.text: Find the bug in this batch update code:
options: The PreparedStatement is created with the correct SQL
addBatch is called correctly for each parameter set
Missing clearBatch() after executeBatch causes stale statements to accumulate
questions.explanation: Without calling clearBatch() after executeBatch(), the batch accumulates stale entries. On the next iteration of the loop, previously added batch entries may be re-executed. Always call clearBatch() after executeBatch() when reusing the same PreparedStatement.

questions.text: Find the bug in this transaction isolation level code:
options: The connection is obtained correctly
setAutoCommit(false) is called to start a transaction
Transaction isolation is set AFTER the transaction starts, having no effect on the current transaction
questions.explanation: setTransactionIsolation() must be called BEFORE setAutoCommit(false). Once a transaction begins, changing the isolation level has no effect on the current transaction. The isolation level is a property of the transaction, not the connection.

questions.text: Find the bug in this savepoint handling code:
options: The savepoint is created correctly
releaseSavepoint is called before rollback, which is the correct order
Using releaseSavepoint after rollbackToSavepoint can cause the savepoint to be unreachable if a later rollback is needed
questions.explanation: After releasing a savepoint with releaseSavepoint(), you cannot rollback to it. If an error occurs later in the transaction and you try to rollback to the released savepoint, it will fail. Keep savepoints alive until the entire transaction commits.

questions.text: Find the bug in this RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS usage:
options: The PreparedStatement is created with RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS correctly
getGeneratedKeys() is called after executeUpdate() correctly
The generated key is read before calling next() on the ResultSet, causing it to point before the first row
questions.explanation: After getGeneratedKeys(), the ResultSet cursor is positioned before the first row. You must call rs.next() before rs.getLong(1) to move to the generated key. Skipping next() results in a JDBC error or incorrect data.

questions.text: Find the bug in this UPDATE statement without WHERE clause:
options: The PreparedStatement is created correctly
The parameter binding is correct
Missing WHERE clause causes all rows in the table to be updated
questions.explanation: An UPDATE without a WHERE clause applies the change to every row in the table. This is one of the most dangerous SQL mistakes — it can corrupt entire tables instantly. Always include a WHERE clause unless you truly intend to update all rows.

questions.text: Find the bug in this GROUP BY query code:
options: The SQL query syntax is valid
The ResultSet processing is correct
SELECT non-aggregated column 'name' not in GROUP BY — produces non-deterministic results in standard SQL
questions.explanation: In standard SQL (and MySQL with strict mode), selecting a column not in GROUP BY that is not aggregated is invalid. PostgreSQL and MySQL strict mode reject this query. Even in MySQL's default mode, the result for 'name' is non-deterministic when multiple names exist per department.

questions.text: Find the bug in this ResultSet cursor handling code:
options: The Connection and PreparedStatement are created correctly
The ResultSet TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE is appropriate for bidirectional scrolling
Calling previous() after next() has reached the end moves cursor to the last row, but using rs.absolute(0) causes an SQLException
questions.explanation: ResultSet cursor positions are 1-based. absolute(0) is not a valid position and throws SQLException. Use absolute(-1) to position before the last row, or absolute(1) for the first row. The valid range for absolute() is 1..N or -1..-N.

questions.text: Find the bug in this HAVING clause usage:
options: The GROUP BY clause is correct
The aggregate function COUNT is used correctly
WHERE is used instead of HAVING to filter on an aggregate function — causes SQL syntax error
questions.explanation: You cannot use WHERE to filter on aggregate functions like COUNT(*). WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. The correct clause is HAVING COUNT(*) > 5. Using WHERE with aggregate functions results in a SQL syntax error.

questions.text: Find the bug in this subquery performance issue:
options: The outer query SELECT clause is correct
The IN subquery is syntactically valid
Correlated subquery executes once per outer row — causes N+1 performance issue with large datasets
questions.explanation: A correlated subquery references the outer query and executes once for each outer row. With 10,000 customers, this runs 10,000 separate queries. Replace with a JOIN or use EXISTS with a proper index for dramatically better performance.

questions.text: Find the bug in this auto-commit configuration:
options: The Connection is obtained from the DataSource correctly
setAutoCommit(false) is called to begin a transaction
Auto-commit is not explicitly set to false before a multi-statement transaction, so each statement commits immediately
questions.explanation: JDBC connections have auto-commit enabled by default. Without calling setAutoCommit(false), each SQL statement is its own transaction and commits immediately. If the second statement fails, the first is already committed, leaving the database in an inconsistent state.

questions.text: Find the bug in this CallableStatement code:
options: The stored procedure call syntax is correct
Output parameter is registered correctly with registerOutParameter
The output parameter is read before execute() is called, returning stale or null data
questions.explanation: Output parameters from CallableStatement are only populated after execute() is called. Reading them before execution returns null or throws an exception because the stored procedure hasn't run yet. Always call cs.execute() before reading OUT parameters.

questions.text: Find the bug in this connection pool configuration:
options: The HikariDataSource is created with the config correctly
maximumPoolSize is set to a reasonable value
connectionTimeout is set to 0 (infinite), which can cause the application to hang indefinitely if the database is down
questions.explanation: A connectionTimeout of 0 means无限等待 — the pool will wait forever for a connection to become available. If the database is down or overloaded, all request threads block indefinitely. Set a reasonable timeout (e.g., 30000ms) so the application fails fast.

questions.text: Find the bug in this MERGE/UPSERT code:
options: The MERGE statement syntax is correct for H2/SQL Server
The ON conflict clause properly identifies the unique constraint
The INSERT part references a column not in the conflict column list, which can cause duplicate key errors on concurrent inserts
questions.explanation: When using MERGE or INSERT ON CONFLICT, the insert values must be consistent with the conflict resolution. If the conflict column is part of a composite unique key but the insert doesn't account for all key columns, concurrent inserts on different non-key columns of the same key group can fail.

questions.text: Find the bug in this PreparedStatement parameter mismatch:
options: The SQL query has 3 parameter placeholders
The first parameter is set correctly with setString
The third parameter is never set — causes a JDBC.SQLException at runtime
questions.explanation: The SQL has 3 placeholders (?,?,?) but only parameters 1 and 2 are set. Parameter 3 is left unset, which throws SQLException when executeQuery is called. Always ensure every placeholder has a corresponding setXxx() call with the correct index.

questions.text: Find the bug in this DataSource connection leak:
options: The DataSource is injected correctly
The connection is obtained and used properly
Connection is not closed in a finally block or try-with-resources — leaks a connection from the pool on every exception
questions.explanation: If an exception occurs between getConnection() and the close() call, the connection is never returned to the pool. With a pool of 10 connections and repeated failures, the pool exhausts and all new requests hang. Use try-with-resources to guarantee cleanup.

questions.text: Find the bug in this JDBC metadata usage:
options: The DatabaseMetaData object is obtained correctly
The column metadata is read properly
Using getColumnName() instead of getColumnLabel() — returns the raw SQL column name, not the AS alias
questions.explanation: getColumnName() returns the actual column name from the table, ignoring any SQL AS alias. getColumnLabel() returns the alias if one is specified. When your SQL uses aliases (e.g., SELECT COUNT(*) AS total), getColumnName() returns '?column?' while getColumnLabel() returns 'total'.

questions.text: Find the bug in this N+1 query pattern in JDBC:
options: The initial query to fetch orders is correct
The inner loop processes each order item correctly
Executing a separate query inside a loop for each order's customer — creates N+1 query problem
questions.explanation: For each order, a separate query fetches the customer data. With 1000 orders, this executes 1001 queries (1 for orders + 1000 for customers). Use a JOIN to fetch all data in one query, or batch-fetch customer IDs and use IN clause.

questions.text: Find the bug in this batch INSERT code:
options: The PreparedStatement is created with the correct SQL
The parameters are set correctly for each row
executeBatch() is called but commit() is never called — in auto-commit=false mode, data is lost
questions.explanation: When auto-commit is disabled, executeBatch() sends the statements to the database but doesn't commit. Without an explicit conn.commit(), the transaction is rolled back when the connection is returned to the pool, and all inserted data is lost.

questions.text: Find the bug in this stored procedure call with cursor:
options: The CallableStatement is created with the correct syntax
The cursor output parameter is registered correctly
The ResultSet from getResultSet() is not closed — leaks the cursor资源 on the database server
questions.explanation: When a stored procedure returns a cursor via CallableStatement, the underlying ResultSet holds a server-side cursor resource. Not closing it leaks that资源 and can eventually exhaust server cursors. Always close the ResultSet in a finally block or try-with-resources.

questions.text: Find the bug in this transaction rollback handling:
options: The transaction is started with setAutoCommit(false) correctly
The savepoint is created correctly
When a SQLException occurs, the code catches it but never calls rollback() — partial changes remain committed
questions.explanation: Even with auto-commit disabled, if an exception is caught without calling rollback(), the connection is returned to the pool with an active uncommitted transaction. The pool may auto-rollback or auto-commit depending on configuration, leading to inconsistent behavior. Always rollback on error.

questions.text: Find the bug in this LEFT JOIN query code:
options: The LEFT JOIN syntax is correct
The parameter binding for the WHERE clause is correct
Using LEFT JOIN but filtering on the right table's column in WHERE — effectively converts it to an INNER JOIN
questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN includes all rows from the left table, even without a match. But when you add WHERE right_table.column IS NOT NULL or WHERE right_table.column = 'value', rows without a match (NULL right side) are filtered out, defeating the purpose of LEFT JOIN. Use the condition in the ON clause instead.

questions.text: Find the bug in this DELETE without WHERE clause:
options: The PreparedStatement creation is correct
The connection handling is correct
Missing WHERE clause deletes ALL rows from the table — catastrophic data loss
questions.explanation: DELETE without WHERE removes every row from the table. This is one of the most destructive SQL mistakes. Always include a WHERE clause unless you intentionally want to truncate the entire table. Consider using TRUNCATE for full-table deletion as it's faster and logged differently.

questions.text: Find the bug in this ResultSet after close attempt:
options: The Connection is obtained correctly
The PreparedStatement is created with a parameterized query
Calling rs.getString() after rs.close() throws SQLException — the code doesn't guard against this
questions.explanation: Once a ResultSet is closed (explicitly or by closing its Statement), any attempt to read from it throws SQLException. The code processes data after closing the ResultSet in a finally block, which always runs first. Order matters: process data BEFORE closing resources.

questions.text: Find the bug in this POST endpoint that creates a resource:
options: The @PostMapping annotation is correct
The request body deserialization is correct
The method returns 200 OK instead of 201 Created — violates HTTP semantics for resource creation
questions.explanation: Per HTTP specification, a successful POST that creates a new resource should return 201 Created, not 200 OK. 201 should include a Location header with the URI of the newly created resource. Using 200 misleads clients about what happened.

questions.text: Find the bug in this PUT endpoint implementation:
options: The @PutMapping annotation is correct for full replacement
The path variable is extracted correctly
Using PUT but only updating non-null fields — this is PATCH semantics, not PUT; PUT requires the full resource representation
questions.explanation: PUT is defined as a complete replacement of the resource. If a client sends a partial representation, the server should either reject it or fill missing fields with defaults. Updating only non-null fields is PATCH behavior. Use @PatchMapping for partial updates.

questions.text: Find the bug in this CORS configuration:
options: The @CrossOrigin annotation is present on the controller
The allowedOrigins is set to a specific domain
Calling addCorsMappings without registering the handler — the CORS config has no effect
questions.explanation: The code creates a WebMvcConfigurer but never registers it with Spring. The addCorsMappings method is never called because the class isn't annotated with @Configuration or registered as a bean. Without registration, CORS remains unconfigured and browsers block cross-origin requests.

questions.text: Find the bug in this ETag caching implementation:
options: The ETag header is generated correctly from the resource version
The If-None-Match header is read from the request correctly
The comparison uses equals() but ETags must be compared after stripping quotes — "abc".equals("\"abc\"") is always false
questions.explanation: HTTP ETags are sent with quotes (e.g., ETag: "abc"). When reading If-None-Match from the request, the value includes quotes. Comparing the raw hash with the quoted header value using equals() always fails. Strip quotes before comparison or use a quoting-aware comparison.

questions.text: Find the bug in this pagination implementation:
options: The Pageable parameter is extracted correctly
The repository call uses Pageable properly
Using offset-based pagination with large datasets — causes performance degradation as offset increases (deep pagination problem)
questions.explanation: Offset-based pagination (LIMIT/OFFSET) requires the database to scan and discard all preceding rows. With offset=100000 and limit=20, the DB reads 100020 rows and discards 100000. For large tables, this is extremely slow. Use cursor-based pagination (keyset pagination) instead.

questions.text: Find the bug in this rate limiting implementation:
options: The rate limit check is performed correctly
The bucket4j限流 logic is sound
Missing Retry-After header in 429 response — clients don't know when to retry
questions.explanation: When returning 429 Too Many Requests, the response should include a Retry-After header indicating how many seconds the client should wait. Without it, clients must guess when to retry, leading to thundering herd problems or excessive waiting.

questions.text: Find the bug in this DELETE endpoint:
options: The @DeleteMapping annotation is correct
The path variable is extracted correctly
Returning 200 OK with body instead of 204 No Content — DELETE should return 204 when no content is returned
questions.explanation: Per HTTP semantics, a successful DELETE that returns no body should use 204 No Content. Returning 200 with a response body is not wrong but is misleading — clients may expect data. Use 204 for successful deletions with no response body.

questions.text: Find the bug in this error handling response:
options: The @ExceptionHandler catches the correct exception type
The method is properly annotated with @RestControllerAdvice
Returning raw exception message to client — exposes internal implementation details and potential security info
questions.explanation: Passing e.getMessage() directly in the error response exposes internal details like SQL queries, stack traces, or file paths. This is a security risk (information disclosure). Always return a generic message and log the full exception server-side.

questions.text: Find the bug in this content negotiation setup:
options: The produces attribute restricts the response content type correctly
The @ResponseBody annotation ensures JSON serialization
The controller returns a String but the client expects JSON — missing produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE
questions.explanation: Without specifying produces, Spring defaults to text/plain for String return types. If the client sends Accept: application/json, Spring cannot serialize a plain String as JSON. Either return an object (which Jackson serializes) or explicitly set produces = APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE and return a JSON-wrapped response.

questions.text: Find the bug in this idempotency implementation:
options: The idempotency key is read from the header correctly
The cache lookup logic is sound
The idempotency key is not stored after first execution — repeated requests with the same key execute again instead of returning cached result
questions.explanation: For idempotency to work, the server must store the result of the first execution keyed by the idempotency key. Without storing the result, every subsequent request with the same key triggers a new execution, defeating the purpose of idempotency for non-idempotent operations like POST.

questions.text: Find the bug in this HATEOAS link generation:
options: The resource representation includes the data correctly
The self link is added with the correct relation type
Missing HATEOAS links for related resources — client must construct URLs manually, breaking REST maturity level 3
questions.explanation: A REST API at HATEOAS maturity (level 3) should include links for all discoverable actions. Without links to related resources (e.g., the user who placed an order), clients must hardcode URL patterns, making the API fragile and violating REST principles.

questions.text: Find the bug in this validation code:
options: The @Valid annotation triggers validation on the request body
The @NotEmpty annotation is correct for string validation
The validation annotations are on the DTO but @Valid is missing on the controller parameter — validation is never triggered
questions.explanation: Without @Valid on the @RequestBody parameter, Spring ignores the Bean Validation annotations on the DTO. The request is deserialized but never validated, allowing invalid data to pass through. Always add @Valid before @RequestBody when validation is required.

questions.text: Find the bug in this API versioning approach:
options: The URL path versioning is clear and explicit
The endpoint mapping is correct
Version in URL path (/api/v1/users) causes URL proliferation — each version duplicates all endpoints; prefer header-based versioning for cleaner URLs
questions.explanation: URL path versioning (/api/v1, /api/v2) duplicates every endpoint URL for each version. This creates maintenance burden and URL bloat. Header-based versioning (Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json) keeps URLs clean and moves versioning to the request metadata where it belongs.

questions.text: Find the bug in this PATCH endpoint:
options: The @PatchMapping annotation is correct for partial updates
The @PathVariable extracts the resource ID correctly
The PATCH handler replaces the entire resource with the partial data — null fields overwrite existing data instead of being ignored
questions.explanation: A PATCH request should only update the fields present in the request. Using objectMapper.convertValue or direct assignment with null values overwrites existing data. Must use merge strategies (e.g., JsonMerger, Optional fields, or manual null checks) to preserve unchanged fields.

questions.text: Find the bug in this cache invalidation code:
options: The cache is correctly populated on GET
The ETag is generated from the resource version
The PUT endpoint updates the resource but doesn't invalidate the cache — stale cached responses are served
questions.explanation: When a resource is updated via PUT/POST/DELETE, any cached responses for that resource become stale. Without explicitly invalidating or evicting the cache entry, subsequent GET requests may return outdated data. Use Cache-Control headers or a cache eviction strategy.

questions.text: Find the bug in this error status code usage:
options: The @ExceptionHandler catches the correct exception type
The response body contains a structured error message
Returning 400 Bad Request for authentication failure — should return 401 Unauthorized
questions.explanation: 400 Bad Request means the request syntax is malformed. Authentication failure (invalid credentials) should return 401 Unauthorized. 403 Forbidden is for when the user is authenticated but lacks permission. Using the wrong status code confuses clients about the actual error.

questions.text: Find the bug in this 304 Not Modified response:
options: The If-None-Match header is read correctly
The ETag comparison logic is sound
Returning 200 OK when ETag matches — should return 304 Not Modified to enable client caching
questions.explanation: When the client sends If-None-Match and the ETag matches, the server should return 304 Not Modified with no body. Returning 200 with the full body defeats the purpose of conditional requests and forces the client to re-process the unchanged response.

questions.text: Find the bug in this N+1 API response building:
options: The endpoint correctly fetches the order
The order items are included in the response
The service method issues a separate query for each order item in a loop — N+1 query problem in the API layer
questions.explanation: For each order, fetching items in a separate query creates N+1 queries. With 50 orders averaging 5 items each, this executes 251 queries. Use JOIN FETCH in JPA, @EntityGraph, or a batch fetch to load all items in one or two queries.

questions.text: Find the bug in this filtering implementation:
options: The filter parameters are extracted correctly
The query construction uses parameterized queries
Filtering via query parameters without sanitization — allows injection of arbitrary WHERE conditions
questions.explanation: Building WHERE clauses by concatenating user-provided filter values directly into SQL strings enables injection attacks. Even with Spring Data, using @Query with SpEL or string interpolation for dynamic filters can be dangerous. Use Specification API or Criteria API for safe dynamic queries.

questions.text: Find the bug in this sorting implementation:
options: The sort parameter is extracted from the query string
The Sort.by() call is constructed correctly
User-provided sort field is passed directly to Sort.by() — allows sorting by arbitrary columns including internal fields
questions.explanation: Passing user-provided field names directly to Sort.by() allows clients to sort by sensitive or unintended columns (e.g., password_hash, internal_id). Always validate the sort field against a whitelist of allowed columns before constructing the Sort object.

questions.text: Find the bug in this redirect implementation:
options: The old endpoint is correctly mapped
The new endpoint URL is correct
Using 302 Found instead of 301 Moved Permanently — search engines don't transfer link equity and clients re-request the old URL
questions.explanation: 302 Found is a temporary redirect — clients and search engines will continue to request the original URL. For permanent URL changes, use 301 Moved Permanently so clients cache the redirect and search engines update their indexes to the new URL.

questions.text: Find the bug in this POST with idempotency key storage:
options: The idempotency key header is read correctly
The cache lookup prevents duplicate processing
The idempotency key is stored in-memory (ConcurrentHashMap) — lost on restart, allowing duplicate executions after server restart
questions.explanation: Storing idempotency keys in-memory means they're lost when the server restarts. If a client retries a request after a restart, the server treats it as a new request and executes it again. Use a persistent store (Redis with TTL, database table) for idempotency keys.

questions.text: Find the bug in this ResponseBody advice:
options: The @RestControllerAdvice annotation is correct
The @ModelAttribute method intercepts all responses
Adding a wrapper to ALL responses including error responses — corrupts the error response format
questions.explanation: ResponseBodyAdvice wraps every response including error responses from @ExceptionHandler. This means error responses get wrapped in the same envelope as successful responses, potentially confusing clients. Use produces filtering or check the response type before wrapping.

questions.text: Find the bug in this streaming response:
options: The Produces media type is set to APPLICATION_NDJSON_VALUE
The StreamingResponseBody is used correctly for async streaming
The objectMapper is called inside the lambda but not thread-safe for concurrent streaming — may produce corrupted JSON
questions.explanation: ObjectMapper instances are not thread-safe for write operations when configuration changes are involved. While a shared ObjectMapper is safe for concurrent reads, if the streaming lambda modifies the mapper's state or if it's not configured immutably, concurrent requests can produce corrupted output.

questions.text: Find the bug in this conditional update (optimistic locking):
options: The version field is correctly annotated with @Version
The If-Match header comparison is performed
The update proceeds even when versions don't match — should return 412 Precondition Failed
questions.explanation: Optimistic locking requires rejecting updates when the resource has been modified since the client last read it. If the client's version doesn't match the current version, the server should return 412 Precondition Failed. Proceeding with the update overwrites concurrent changes silently.

questions.text: Find the bug in this git operation in Java code:
options: The ProcessBuilder setup is correct for running git commands
The command arguments are properly separated
Using git push --force on a shared branch — overwrites other developers' commits and causes data loss
questions.explanation: Force pushing (--force) to a shared branch overwrites commits that others may have based their work on. This causes data loss and forces other developers to manually fix their local branches. Use --force-with-lease instead, which fails if the remote has commits you don't have locally.

questions.text: Find the bug in this git rebase operation:
options: The ProcessBuilder is configured correctly
The branch name parameter is extracted correctly
Performing rebase on a public/shared branch — rewrites published commit history, causing conflicts for collaborators
questions.explanation: Rebase rewrites commit history by creating new commits. On a public branch, this means collaborators' local history diverges from the remote, causing repeated conflicts and confusion. Rule: never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch.

questions.text: Find the bug in this stash apply code:
options: The git stash save command is executed correctly
The ProcessBuilder setup is correct
Using git stash apply without checking if stash exists — throws an error if no stash entries are available
questions.explanation: git stash apply fails with 'No stash entries found' if the stash list is empty. The code doesn't check the exit code of the save command or verify stash list before applying. Always check if there are stash entries before applying, and handle the case where apply fails due to conflicts.

questions.text: Find the bug in this cherry-pick implementation:
options: The commit SHA is passed correctly
The ProcessBuilder is configured correctly
Cherry-picking without checking for conflicts — the code proceeds even if the cherry-pick fails due to merge conflicts
questions.explanation: Cherry-pick can fail if the commit conflicts with the current branch. The code checks exitCode == 0 but doesn't handle the conflict state (git cherry-pick --continue or --abort). If conflicts occur, the repository is left in a dirty state with unresolved merge markers.

questions.text: Find the bug in this git bisect automation:
options: The bisect start command is correct
The good and bad commits are specified correctly
The test script exit code is inverted — git bisect expects exit 0 for good and non-zero for bad, but the script returns 1 for good
questions.explanation: git bisect run expects the test script to exit with code 0 (or 1-124) for 'good' and 125+ for 'skip', non-zero for 'bad'. If the script inverts this (returns non-zero for good), bisect goes in the wrong direction and identifies the wrong commit as the first bad one.

questions.text: Find the bug in this git hook registration:
options: The hook file path is constructed correctly
The hook script content is written to the file
The hook file is not set as executable — git ignores hooks that don't have execute permission
questions.explanation: Git requires hook scripts to have execute permission (chmod +x). Without it, git silently ignores the hook. On Windows, this is less relevant (git uses its own hook mechanism), but on Linux/Mac the hook simply won't run. Always set file permissions after writing the hook.

questions.text: Find the bug in this .gitignore pattern:
options: The pattern correctly ignores compiled classes
The pattern correctly ignores log files
The pattern *.env ignores ALL .env files including those in subdirectories that should be tracked
questions.explanation: The pattern *.env ignores .env files at any level. If you need to track a .env.example or .env.template for documentation, this pattern prevents it. Use more specific patterns like .env (root only) or .env.local for files that should be ignored, and negate specific ones with !.env.example.

questions.text: Find the bug in this git shallow clone operation:
options: The --depth parameter limits clone history correctly
The repository URL is specified correctly
Shallow clone with --depth=1 prevents git blame from working across the full history — blame only shows the most recent commit for each line
questions.explanation: A shallow clone with --depth=1 only fetches the latest commit. git blame, git log, and git bisect all depend on full history. With a shallow clone, blame shows only the shallowest commit for each line, making it useless for understanding code evolution. Use --depth=1 only for CI builds, not development.

questions.text: Find the bug in this submodule initialization:
options: The git clone command is correct
The recursive flag ensures nested submodules are cloned
After cloning, submodules are not initialized — code assumes submodule directories contain files but they're empty
questions.explanation: git clone with --recursive clones and initializes submodules. However, if the initial clone was without --recursive, the submodule directories exist but are empty. You must run git submodule init && git submodule update to populate them. The code assumes files exist after clone without verifying submodule state.

questions.text: Find the bug in this signed commit verification:
options: The git log format string is correct
The GPG signature check is performed
Using git log --format='%G?' checks signature but the code doesn't handle the case where the commit is NOT signed (shows 'N' for no signature)
questions.explanation: git log --format='%G?' outputs 'G' for good signature, 'B' for bad signature, 'U' for untrusted, and 'N' for no signature. The code only checks for 'G' but treats 'N' (unsigned) as acceptable. An attacker can push unsigned commits that bypass verification. Reject 'N' commits in security-critical repos.

questions.text: Find the bug in this git reflog cleanup code:

Creating a lightweight tag instead of annotated — lightweight tags lack metadata (author, date, message) needed for release tracking
questions.explanation: Lightweight tags (git tag <name>) are just pointers to a commit with no metadata. Annotated tags (git tag -a <name> -m <msg>) store the tagger name, email, date, and a message. For releases, always use annotated tags — they're required for git describe and contain release information.

Sparse checkout ignores .gitignore patterns — files excluded by .gitignore may still appear in the sparse checkout
questions.explanation: Sparse checkout and .gitignore are independent mechanisms. Sparse checkout controls which files are in the working tree; .gitignore controls which files git tracks. A file can be in the sparse checkout but ignored by .gitignore, or tracked but not in the sparse checkout. Both need to be configured correctly.

Using --prune without --all fetches only the default remote — stale branches from other remotes are not cleaned up
questions.explanation: git fetch --prune only cleans stale branches from the default remote (origin). If the repository has multiple remotes, stale branches from other remotes persist. Use git fetch --all --prune to clean all remotes, or explicitly specify the remote.

questions.explanation: git branch -d refuses to delete a branch with unmerged commits (safety feature). If the branch has work that hasn't been merged, the command fails silently. Use -D (force delete) only when you're certain the work is no longer needed, or merge it first.

Using rebase on a feature branch that has already been pushed — rewrites pushed commits, causing force-push requirement and collaboration issues
questions.explanation: Rebasing a branch that's already been pushed to a shared remote rewrites commit history. Collaborators who have based work on those commits will face conflicts. If the branch is shared, use merge. Only rebase local branches that haven't been shared yet.

questions.explanation: git reset --hard HEAD~1 moves the branch pointer back, discarding the latest commit and all uncommitted changes. On a shared branch, this rewrites history that others may have based work on. Use git revert (creates a new commit that undoes changes) for shared branches.
